news.text:
The Supreme Court delivered another victory for President Trump on the issue of illegal migration on Monday. The High Court reversed a decision by an Obama-appointed judge that had blocked the termination of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for illegal aliens from Venezuela.

But “temporary” is the key word here; beneficiaries of the TPS program are allowed to remain only for a while before returning home, yet Justice Alito observed that “TPS designations in practice have often lasted for decades.”

Trump has successfully terminated 13 of the 17 designations, and on June 25 the Supreme Court upheld Trump’s authority to shut these programs down in Mullin v. Doe. This set a clear precedent for Trump to terminate the remaining TPS programs, too.

news.title: Trump Makes Scathing Gesture After Question He Won’t Answer
news.text:
President Donald Trump has repeatedly refused to answer questions about his shocking casual comment surrounding Los Angeles and San Diego.

Trump, 80, was discussing his war with Iran that has led to sky-high oil prices at a rally in Nebraska on Monday. 

“It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe,” he continued, before appearing to suggest that he would accept the destruction of the two U.S. cities. “They can take out a city—let ’em take, let ’em take out Los Angeles, let ’em take out San Diego. That’s—this is a very small price to pay,” Trump said, naming the two Democrat-led cities in California.

The comments immediately raised eyebrows. California Governor Gavin Newsom posted on X shortly afterward, “Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego. He is deranged and dangerous.”

The senior president was seemingly in no mood to expand on his comments at the White House on Tuesday, after returning from a speech in Maryland.

A female journalist asked him as he walked toward her, “Mr. President, what did you mean by your comments yesterday about San Diego and Los Angeles possibly being wiped out by Iran?” 

Trump made a swatting gesture with his hand, and refused to answer the question.

Hours earlier on Tuesday, before he headed to Maryland, Trump also ignored reporters who asked him to explain the baffling comment. 

The White House has tried to dismiss the claim as a “hoax.” The Rapid Response X account shared footage of Trump avoiding the reporter’s question, adding, “Some whiny Fake News loser spent the entire press gaggle shouting at @POTUS about the ‘take out Los Angeles and San Diego’ hoax — which is so obviously a lie, even CNN debunked it. These people are sick.” 

The post seemingly referred to CNN fact checker Daniel Dale saying Trump had been paraphrased by the Kamala Harris-linked Headquarters account on X.

Speaking on CNN’s Anderson Cooper 360°, Kaitlan Collins said she and other White House reporters on Tuesday had “tried to ask the president to clarify those comments, or explain what he meant,” on three separate occasions.

“When you look at the transcript and the audio of what he said there, he obviously heard the questions,” Collins told Cooper, noting Trump “declined to answer them.”

When asked for a comment, White House Communications Director Stephen Cheung sent the Daily Beast his earlier X post, which read, “The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality. He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped. America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money.”

Officials, however, aren’t convinced. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass slammed Trump on Tuesday’s 360°, saying she was “horrified” by them. She also called out the White House response.

“I mean, I heard what I heard, and so did the rest of the world. What does that say about the United States on the world stage. that the president would say, ‘If you want to take out the nation’s second largest city, have at it’,” Bass told Cooper on CNN.

“I understand that that press deputy wanted to paint it that way, as though we did not hear what we heard. But I’m sorry to say that it is on tape, and the entire world heard it.”

news.title: 'The View' co-host Ana Navarro offers one key reason for why she still identifies as a Republican
news.text: Former Republican strategist and vocal critic of President Donald Trump Ana Navarro explained to actor Michael Douglas on Tuesday's "The View" that she only stays registered as a Republican voter so she can influence the primaries in Florida. "I have to ask you something," Douglas began. "I've admired you now so much for the last couple of years … But why aren't you independent? How can you still be a Republican?" Navarro, her co-hosts and the audience erupted in laughter. "I'll tell you why, because I live in Florida where the primaries are closed, and I want to be able to vote in the primaries and vote against those sons of b----es," Navarro said, adding, she hoped to "make a difference in the primaries." ABC'S 'THE VIEW' CO-HOST ANA NAVARRO URGES VIEWERS TO VOTE FOR DEM IN KEY FLORIDA CONGRESSIONAL RACE Over the years, Navarro has faced criticism from conservatives for identifying as a Republican while advocating for many of the same policies as her left-leaning co-hosts. Navarro also was a host at the 2024 Democratic National Convention and supported former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. During an interview this week with Entertainment Weekly, Navarro addressed those criticisms directly. "I’d argue that anybody who espouses the same views as Donald Trump isn’t much of a traditional Republican," Navarro said. "I’m not going to be lectured to about what a Republican is or isn’t." 'THE VIEW' HOST ANA NAVARRO BOYCOTTS WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENTS’ DINNER, SAYS 'NO WAY IN HELL' In 2019, Navarro explained to her co-hosts that she had previously supported former Florida Governor Jeb Bush's 2016 presidential bid, noting she identifies as an "old-fashioned Republican." When a co-host pressed her for more details on what this means, Navarro said she believed in free trade, strong foreign policy, and is "pro-immigration." This point of debate came up again in 2022 when she was confronted by co-host Sunny Hostin, over why she still sees herself as a Republican. "Why are you still a Catholic?" responded Navarro. "You don’t agree with everything about the Catholic Church." Last month, ABC and "The View" faced scrutiny after Navarro urged viewers to vote for a Democratic candidate in a key congressional race in Florida. "Ana Navarro doesn’t represent a broader phenomenon of GOP dissidents; she represents a total grift," she said. "She hasn’t supported anything from her supposed party in over a decade, but she won’t surrender her Republican voting card because it’s a credential that gets her on news programs." news.title: Mike Johnson reveals one of his ‘top three’ battleground House races
news.text:
“The entire country is watching what happens in about four districts in Pennsylvania, and this is a top three race in America right now,” Johnson said. “So, you’re not just supporting local law enforcement and the 7th District of Pennsylvania — you’re supporting the American way.”

The event is part of a dizzying schedule for Johnson, who is attempting to defy electoral history and preserve Republicans’ wafer-thin control of the House. Johnson will travel to 40 more districts between now and Election Day and has competitive races in four other states — Wisconsin, Michigan, Ohio, and Iowa — on his itinerary for this week alone.

In Pennsylvania, Johnson campaigned on behalf of Mackenzie, but also Reps. Scott Perry (R-PA), Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA), and Rob Bresnahan (R-PA) on Tuesday. All of their races are rated as competitive or true toss-ups by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report and could on their own decide which party controls the majority next year.

Mackenzie eked out a 1-percentage-point win in his 2024 race, but as of now trails Democratic challenger Bob Brooks by 5 points in the latest public polling. In 2024, President Donald Trump carried the seat by 3 percentage points over former Vice President Kamala Harris.

“This is going to be a close election — we all know that,” Johnson told the Washington Examiner at the campaign event, before predicting that Republicans would win on a message that draws a contrast between “common sense and crazy.”

Working against Republicans this election cycle are the political headwinds that ordinarily come with being the party in power, as well as a war in Iran that has weighed down Trump’s approval ratings.

There is concern that Republicans do not have a strong top of the ticket in Pennsylvania, with polls showing Gov. Josh Shapiro (D-PA) ahead of GOP challenger Stacy Garrity by as much as 27 points.

As a result, Mackenzie is banking on voters to split their ticket and said there is precedent for them doing so in past elections.

“Those coattails don’t necessarily extend, and that’s because we have a very informed, very educated electorate,” he said. “They are swing voters. They like to go race by race, candidate by candidate.”

“I’m confident we’re going to see that again,” he added.

news.title: Three Senate Races Shift Toward Democrats with Midterms 4 Weeks Away
news.text: Three Senate races have just shifted in favor of Democrats four weeks ahead of the midterm elections as Republicans are attempting to maintain their control. The Cook Political Report has moved Kansas' race from Lean Republican to a Toss Up, New Hampshire from a Toss Up to Lean Democrat and North Carolina from Lean Democrat to Likely Democrat. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. Republicans now hold a narrow majority in both the House and Senate. President Donald Trump carried Kansas by double digits over then-Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election, underscoring the state’s Republican tilt. But Democrats have maintained a foothold in the state, with Laura Kelly in the governor’s mansion even as Republicans hold both U.S. Senate seats. Trump also won North Carolina in the 2024 election and Harris won New Hampshire. The new shifts add to already worrisome signs for Republicans as Democrats hope to capitalize on Trump's souring approval ratings and as affordability concerns rise across American households. "At this point, the question isn’t whether Democrats will gain seats, but how many," the forecaster said in part. What To Know Cook now estimates Democrats will pick up two to six Senate seats, as the party needs four to take control. Cook highlights that Republicans remain hopeful in Michigan and Maine, but the momentum is against the president's party as Election Day nears. In Kansas, the GOP could lose the seat held by Republicans since 1919, the longest ever for any party, High Plains Public Radio says. The position is currently held by Republican incumbent Senator Roger Marshall, a doctor, who is battling Democrat Adam Hamilton for the seat. According to recent polling, Hamilton either leads by a very slim margin or the race is statistically tied. The forecaster previously highlighted that agriculture—and economic concerns impacting fertilizer and gas—are major factors in the Sunflower State and the rising prices make the race more competitive. Cook labeled the race "Democrats’ Cinderella story of the cycle." Prediction market site Kalshi shows Marshall in the lead on Tuesday afternoon, as does Polymarket. In New Hampshire, Democrat Chris Pappas is leading over Republican John E. Sununu in the battle for the U.S. Senate seat. The forecaster points to recent polling as the reason for the shift but says, "This race could still end up being closer than it should be given the national environment." Notably, the state has not elected a Republican senator in more than 15 years. Sununu represented the Granite State in the Senate from 2003 to 2009. Kalshi and Polymarket show Pappas in the lead on Tuesday afternoon. In North Carolina, Republican nominee Michael Whatley is trailing behind former Governor Roy Cooper in a slew of polls. Recently, Trump vocalized his concerns about Whatley as the Senate Leadership Fund paused advertising for the race to redirect resources elsewhere. Trump held a rally for Whatley in the Tar Heel State last month as the president vowed to campaign across the country for Republicans in the lead-up to November. Democrats have not won a U.S. Senate election in the state in about 18 years. Kalshi and Polymarket show Cooper ahead of Whatley on Tuesday afternoon. Democrats are hoping to capitalize on Trump's dropping approval ratings in state and national polls as the midterm elections loom. The president's overall approval and ranking on key policy issues like the economy, immigration, jobs and the ongoing war in Iran have slipped as households across America are flagging affordability concerns. Robert Y. Shapiro, professor of political science at the School of International and Public Affairs at Columbia, told Newsweek on Tuesday, "It is clear that on almost all fronts the election is moving in the direction of the Democrats taking the House and very possibly the Senate." Shapiro added: "On the Senate side they have to hold on to Minnesota, Michigan, and New Hampshire where the Republicans are in play, which will keep the matter of control of the Senate tight for the Democrats. Polls on overall voting for Congress are solidly in the Democrats favor at an 8 point lead or better, and the most telling trend showing that the election may be a very strong refutation of Trump and Republican leadership is that Trump's performance rating has fallen noticeably among Republicans, with continued tanking among Independent voters." news.text:
“HMP and Republicans are in agreement—Democrats are on offense and are taking back the House,” HMP National Press Secretary Katarina Flicker told the Washington Examiner.

Here are the races where the groups have slashed or withdrawn advertising:

Nebraska’s 2nd District

Both the GOP and Democratic super PACs have pulled spending from Nebraska’s 2nd Congressional District. Republicans have cut more than $1.1 million in television ads from the seat.

The Omaha-based district has trended blue in recent years and was one of the toughest seats for Republicans to keep this cycle after Rep. Don Bacon (R-NE) announced his retirement. This seat was one of three GOP-held seats that former Vice President Kamala Harris won in 2024.

Democrat Denise Powell is leading Republican Brinker Harding in a spate of recent polls.

New Jersey’s 9th District

AdImpact shows Republicans cutting just under $200,000 from New Jersey’s 9th Congressional District. The seat is held by first-term Democratic Rep. Nellie Pou (D-NJ). CLF denies it pulled money from the race, saying rather that it was just allocated in the New York media market.

In 2024, Pou won the seat by 5 percentage points even as President Donald Trump narrowly carried it by a point over Harris. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report shifted the seat to increasingly favor Democrats.

New York’s 19th and 3rd districts

Republicans have also pulled over $1.4 million in broadcast ads in New York’s 19th Congressional District, where Rep. Josh Riley (D-NY) is running for reelection. Riley flipped the seat from Republicans in 2024 and has outraised his GOP challenger, state senator Peter Oberacker, this cycle handily.

New York’s 19th District voted for Harris over Trump by a narrow 1 percentage point in 2024.

AdImpact also shows that Republicans pulled nearly $100,000 from New York’s 3rd Congressional District. Rep. Tom Suozzi (D-NY) is running for reelection in the seat against former state assemblyman Mike LiPetri. Trump carried the seat narrowly over Harris in 2024.

The GOP money pulled out of New York’s 3rd District is being reallocated to ads in New Jersey’s 7th Congressional District, where Rep. Tom Kean (R-NJ) is facing a competitive reelection challenge. Trump carried the seat by 2 points in 2024.

CLF denies it pulled money from New York’s 3rd District, saying rather that it was just allocated in the New York media market.

California’s 48th District

Democrats pulled over $200,000 from California’s 48th Congressional District. The new seat is open after Rep. Darrell Issa (R-CA) was redrawn by a Democratic gerrymander following the passage of Proposition 50 last year in an effort to create a Democratic pickup opportunity.

Democrat Marni von Wilpert will face Republican Jim Desmond in November. If the seat existed in 2024, it would have voted for Harris by 3 points over Trump.

Michigan’s 8th District

While Republicans still have TV time booked in Michigan’s 8th Congressional District, Democrats have pulled nearly $200,000. They say the move is a signal of confidence in Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-MI).

Rivet is running against Tom Smith, who bested President Donald Trump’s handpicked candidate in the GOP primary, despite having quit the race a month prior.

news.title: The danger of calling the left stupid
news.text:
A long list of prominent conservatives have referred to leftists and Democrats as dumb, stupid, incompetent, crazy, and insane. In 2007, Ann Coulter wrote the book “If Democrats Had Any Brains, They’d Be Republicans.” Both Rush Limbaugh and President Trump regularly referred to Democrats as “Dumbocrats.” More recently, the leader of the House Freedom Caucus called Democrats “the crazy party,” and JD Vance framed the contrast between the parties as “common sense vs. crazy.”

Matt Margolis titled a piece in PJ Media this year “Democrats Are Too Stupid to Heed This Warning” and posited that somewhere between the 1990s and today, the Democratic Party lost its mind. Some of this stuff gets a chuckle, but conservatives need to be careful with this narrative.

Calling an adversary’s actions crazy or stupid implies that those actions produce an outcome fundamentally different from what their architects intended.

Conservatives need to understand that this tactic can not only contradict the more serious messages they’re trying to convey about leftist policies, it can also remove responsibility from leftists for their malevolence.

Consider a recent interview in which Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) explained that the left’s open-border policy was part of a shrewd, long-term plan to bring in new Democrat constituents, with sanctuary-city policies as another step in that plan. Yet in the same interview, he called the policy “just stupid” and “one of the dumbest policies I’ve ever heard of,” and, in a later interview, adding that “just about every single position today’s left adopts is crazy.”

So we are told that leftists are shrewd, long-term planners who are simultaneously stupid and crazy. Which is it? The distinction may seem trivial, but it’s not.

We need to distinguish between leftist leadership and its dominant agenda on the one hand and its useful idiots on the other.

To be clear, there are certainly some dim bulbs among the left — both in leadership and rank and file. Showcase examples include Vice President Kamala Harris, who frequently struggles to articulate coherent sentences; Rep. Hank Johnson (D-Ga.), who worried during a congressional hearing that Guam might “tip over and capsize” if it became too populated; and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), who told us that America with defunded police would look just like the wealthy white suburbs.

On a broader scale, consider millions of California voters who knowingly continue to vote for politicians whose policies have devastated the Golden State.

But these examples aside, the overarching leftist agenda — and the people who genuinely understand, subscribe to, and orchestrate it — cannot simply be dismissed as stupid. Doing so is dangerous.

The rise of the New Left

As has often been the case with radical leftist movements in the United States, their stated objective is to dismantle existing American institutions, traditions, and governing structures in favor of a fundamentally different social order. Put simply, they despise America as it currently exists.

Once you understand this premise, their positions look less like harebrained, stupid, illogical, or unworkable ideas, but more like carefully conceived, sometimes ingenious tactics intended to advance that larger objective.

RELATED: Democrats are desperate to 'Europe' our health care system

 Sorbetto/Getty Images

In this light, things like defunding the police, draconian regulations and carbon taxes, mothballing coal and nuclear plants, wide-open borders, turning a blind eye to Medicaid and NGO fraud, supporting genital mutilation of minors, opposing voter ID, massive expansion of entitlement spending, lowering combat readiness standards in the military in the name of gender equality, and support for adversaries like Hamas can be understood not as disconnected examples of incompetence, but as elements of a broader ideological program.

If it does damage to America and hastens the great realignment, they support it.

Whether one agrees with that interpretation of any particular policy is a separate question. The important point is that conservatives shouldn’t automatically assume destructive policies are the product of stupidity.

In “America’s Cultural Revolution,” Christopher Rufo explains how the radical left’s approach evolved from traditional Marxist class conflict toward an emphasis on race, gender, and identity. Traditional Marxism defined the conflict largely in socioeconomic terms, pitting the working class against the wealthy. In the United States, however, the middle class proved too large, mobile, and invested in the existing system for a conventional class-based revolution to take hold.

Influenced by thinkers such as Antonio Gramsci and Herbert Marcuse, the New Left increasingly emphasized “the war of position,” “the long march through the institutions,” and racial and cultural identity as alternatives to direct political conflict. Barack Obama became a highly consequential figure in this transformation.

During his 2008 presidential campaign, Obama told an audience in Columbia, Missouri, “We are five days away from fundamentally transforming the United States of America.” In the years that followed, he did precisely that.

The media proactively escalated the new narrative, increasing use of the terms racist, racists, and racism by roughly 700% between 2011 and 2019. The phrase “white supremacy” rarely appeared in the media until 2015, but by 2019, the Times and the Post were using it 17 to 18 times more often than in 2014, with similar jumps for “systemic racism,” “white privilege,” “unconscious bias,” and “whiteness.”

Gallup found that the share of respondents who believed black-white relations were “very good” or “somewhat good” plummeted from about 70% to 47% by 2015.

From the perspective of those who designed it, this was a deliberate and consequential political strategy. Arthur Brooks put it well, pointing out that the president ran on optimism and unity but governed on pessimism and division. In 2011, Obama’s Executive Order 13583 cemented DEI language, metrics, and policies across federal agencies. The resulting fallout has been well documented.

RELATED: The right is building its own lawfare defense machine — finally

 Schöning/ullstein bild/Getty Images

Stupid or strategic?

To call leftist leaders or their policies stupid is therefore more than an unfortunate choice of words. It can mislead conservatives regarding what they are confronting.

We don’t tend to think of stupid people as evil. Perceived stupidity neutralizes perceived intent and, to some degree, perceived blame. “Stupid” is not the word that comes to mind for figures like Stalin, Mao, or Pol Pot, and it would have done us no favors to describe the Axis powers in World War II as merely stupid or crazy.

Calling an adversary’s actions crazy or stupid implies that those actions produce an outcome fundamentally different from what their architects intended. But what if the opposite is true? What if the policies are producing precisely the disruption their architects sought?

Once upon a time, Democrats and Republicans were two parties with broadly similar hopes for America but sharply different views on how to get there. That time has passed.

Conservatives should not lose sight of what they believe to be the left’s overarching mission. They need to describe political actions, and the consequences those actions produce, not simply as the unfortunate results of incompetent or stupid people, but as those of an underlying ideological agenda.

That doesn’t mean every Democrat is a radical leftist, every leftist is an intellectual strategist, or every controversial policy reflects a coordinated conspiracy. Nor does it mean conservatives should stop pointing out genuinely foolish statements or incompetent decisions. It means something simpler: Stop confusing foolishness with strategy.

Some political actors may indeed be foolish. Others may be highly intelligent and deeply committed to an ideological vision conservatives regard as destructive. Those two categories shouldn’t be confused.

If conservatives want to understand and effectively challenge the modern left, they should focus less on calling its leaders stupid and more on understanding what they’re trying to accomplish. That leadership may be insidious, duplicitous, destructive, morally wrong, and in some cases evil. But dismissing them as stupid or crazy risks missing the point entirely.

Let’s start calling them out on what they actually intend to do.

About Anthony Allred II 

Anthony Allred is an Executive Producer and Creative and Talent Executive with more than a decade of experience producing original content and securing high-profile talent across television, digital, social and live programming. He began his entertainment career at BET’s flagship music and entertainment program 106 & Park before joining REVOLT TV, where he served as a Senior Producer on Revolt Live. news.title: Is the Swiftie army finally thinning out? Allie Beth Stuckey thinks she knows why
news.text:
Is Taylor Swift’s colossal fanbase finally beginning to dwindle? BlazeTV host Allie Beth Stuckey sees the writing on the wall, and it doesn’t look good for the global pop star. While Swift is coming off a record-breaking album and a very public marriage, her latest release has even some faithful Swifties wincing.

On this episode of “Relatable,” Allie sits down with former producer and longtime Swift fan Bri Schrader to have an honest conversation about Swift’s latest album release, whether or not it forebodes doom, and what Swift’s sudden “trad” shift may point to.

“So Taylor Swift released basically the deluxe version of her album ‘The Life of a Showgirl’ ... and everyone's talking about it because some of the songs are controversial,” says Bri.

She explains that the original album was already controversial because even hardcore fans thought it was “bad writing.” The four added songs only worsened matters.

Allie notes that “The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore” has a Metacritic score of “39 out of 100” — the “first red album” of Swift’s career.

“And then, we also have Poppie Platt, a reviewer for the Telegraph. She titled her review, ‘I'm a Swiftie, and even I think these songs are terrible.’ ... She said that what [Swift] doesn't seem to have realized is that the music must be good to do a surprise release,” Allie continues.

“Do you think, as some people are speculating, that she has lost her artistic edge since meeting Travis?” she asks.

“I love Taylor Swift, but I have felt that almost every song that's been about him has just not been her strongest lyrically. And so has she lost her edge? I don't know. I mean, maybe,” says Bri.

“She wrote a whole album about concepts and stories that aren't even hers or related to her and that was my favorite album of hers, and so I think she's still able to tap into that. So maybe it's just the songs that are strictly about [Travis] that are kind of meh to me,” she continues, noting that people are specifically “clowning on” Swift’s song “Cleveland,” which is about Kelce taking her to see his hometown.

Bri believes Swift has entered a new era. “She's in this phase right now that's very like, ‘Oh, screw the haters. I found my man, and he plays football.’ She has, like, five songs that are just basically that,” she says, “and I think that's what I'm tired of a little bit.”

“You would think she'd be more popular than ever having this football husband, having gotten married, obviously being excited about getting married,” says Allie. 

“Maybe it's because she's moved even more. I mean, obviously she was always mainstream ... but she's gone into other realms that typically maybe don't think about Taylor Swift ... and now people just feel a need to always commentate on her life or her politics.”

“I feel like people are more annoyed with her in general than in seasons past in her life.”

Bri agrees that Swift’s public perception is shifting. “There's a section of people who have always not liked her, who have always thought she was cheesy and annoying. Then there's the people, I think, who were turned off by this album specifically,” she says, explaining how certain songs expressing desire for marriage and motherhood were criticized for being too traditional.

“People are now like, ‘OK, so she's going to be a little trad now,’ and that's annoying to a lot of the people who liked her before,” Bri continues. “So I think those things combined, she's just at levels of annoying for most people right now, which is unfortunate for her.”

Allie believes Swift’s sudden shift to traditionalism is less about a real change of heart and more about political influence.

“Her and the Kelces are all a part of a psyop. ... I'm not saying that it's not real, but they represent what Democrats want to convey — that you can be a progressive feminist who likes Kamala Harris and hates Donald Trump and you're from the Midwest, you represent normal Americans, you can be trad, you can have kids,” she speculates.

“But I think when presidential election time comes around that the Kelce-Swift combo is going to be flexing their influence muscles for the Democrats.”

In their crosshairs, she argues, will be a very specific demographic: “that white suburban mom ... that instinctively doesn't like Trump but is also kind of trad.”

“And I think the more trad she gets and the more she remains progressive in other ways, the more they think that she's going to be able to persuade people over to their side. ... She's playing a long ideological game here,” says Allie.

To hear more, watch the episode above.

Want more from Allie Beth Stuckey?

To enjoy more of Allie’s upbeat and in-depth coverage of culture, news, and theology from a Christian, conservative perspective, subscribe to BlazeTV — the largest multi-platform network of voices who love America, defend the Constitution, and live the American dream.

news.title: Democrats debate Kamala Harris 2028 run as surrogate says party wants to 'move on' from 2024 loss
news.text: Allies of former Vice President Kamala Harris, as well as Democratic surrogates, are questioning whether the former Democratic nominee would be the top choice within the party, weighing her name recognition and respect among Democrats against the notion that voters want to move on. "People just want to move on," Fletcher Smith, a former state legislator in South Carolina and Biden 2020 surrogate, told The Washington Post. "We’ve got a number of younger generation of people who are capable of leading — we’ve got governors, we’ve got congresspeople, we have senators. I think what she needs to do is sit out 2028 and let some other people have a shot at saving our democracy." Many Democratic allies noted Harris is well respected within the party, but questioned whether respect translated into support. DEMOCRATS SHY AWAY FROM QUESTIONS ON WHETHER HARRIS SHOULD RUN FOR PRESIDENT IN 2028 "She’s extraordinarily popular in the party and people are very fond of her and want her to be treated with a lot of respect and deference — given all the due of someone in her position," Jamal Simmons, a former communications director for Harris, told the Post. "Many people see it as a service what she did in 2024, where she really stepped up for the party, stepped up for Joe Biden, stepped up for the country. There’s a lot of respect for her. But it’s yet to be seen how much of that becomes support for another presidential run." Podcast host and former South Carolina state senator Bakari Sellers told the Post that though she is" very talented," she has yet to define what a potential 2028 run would look like to key constituencies. "One of the first statements she put out was about AI, when it’s clear she needs to boost her support among Black men," Sellers told the Post. "California has a cost-of-living issue, and she’s not talking about cost of living at all." The Post reported that Sellers said he hasn't spoken to Harris in over a year. He suggested that was concerning for a candidate who would need a victory in South Carolina, according to the report. HARRIS STOPS IN KEY PRESIDENTIAL PRIMARY STATE AFTER LEAVING DOOR WIDE OPEN TO 2028 RUN During Sellers' podcast on Monday, he listed Harris as No. 2 in his top five candidates for 2028. He said Harris was talented and intelligent, but questioned whether her team would "let her be great." "Let Kamala be Kamala, and you would have the next president of the United States without a doubt in my mind," he said. The podcast host ranked Maryland Gov. Wes Moore in the No. 1 spot, calling him the "biggest impediment" to Harris being the nominee. WATCH: DEM SENATORS DODGE BACKING KAMALA HARRIS IN POTENTIAL 2028 RUN: ‘VERY MESSY’ Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff, who was part of Hillary Clinton's 2016 campaign, told Fox News Digital that Harris hasn't done anything differently since 2024. "Harris has not done anything truly new or different since 2024. Her greatest post-VP visibility came from her book tour. Running again without a new chapter or story to tell is like reapplying to the same college after getting rejected, taking a gap year, and coming back with basically the same application. You can rewrite the essay, but if you did nothing new, admissions is still looking at the same file," Shroff said. Shroff suggested somebody new might have the advantage over her because they would be introducing themselves to voters for the first time on a national stage. "She does not get to reintroduce herself. That is the burden of being so well known. She has a real base and a lot of goodwill in the party, but she also lost, and that makes some voters and, importantly, donors nervous. Even if she starts high in the polls, the question is where the growth comes from if there is not much new to add," he said. "Someone like a Pritzker at least gets the advantage of telling his story to a lot of voters for the first time." Shroff added, "What Harris is doing well right now is using her position as a party leader rather than acting like a candidate in waiting. A great example is her showing up for Abdul El-Sayed despite his criticism of her and the bad blood with some on the far left in Michigan. She acknowledged the disagreements, still made the case for him, and used her stature to help unite the party in a critical moment — particularly with outreach to Black voters. That is an example of influence she has right now, regardless of what she does in 2028 and that will continue to matter whether she seeks the nomination or not." California Gov. Gavin Newsom said during a recent interview that he would not run in 2028 if Harris planned to run. DEM MEGADONOR UNLEASHES REALITY CHECK ON HARRIS FOR 2028 WHILE EYEING SOCIALIST FIREBRAND Harris has not been definitive on whether she plans to run, but has said she is thinking about it. Others were more confident in Harris, including Ashley Etienne, another former communications director for the former VP. She told the Post that Harris would need to separate herself from the Democratic establishment, but said she would have major advantages in a national election. CARVILLE DOESN'T 'FEEL SORRY' FOR URGING DEMOCRATS TO MOVE ON FROM THE KAMALA HARRIS ERA "It’s almost like, why not her? She has proven, unlike anyone else in the race, that she’s got these advantages that will matter in a national election," she told the Post. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Virginia Democratic state senator L. Louise Lucas told the Post that Democrats rejecting Harris too fast could be interpreted as a negative political move as well, suggesting it could be seen as overlooking a qualified Black woman for the position. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "There’s no question that people would be upset because you see what happened last time," Lucas told the Post. "It could very well be that some folks would be so disillusioned that they would just say, ‘I give up on this process’ — especially people who’ve been fighting as many years as I have, who have come through the civil rights movement and just experienced so much, endured so much, and then to see this happen again would be quite painful." Several members of Congress didn't rush to throw their support behind Harris when asked by Fox News Digital about her possibly running in 2028. "Well, I've backed her before, but there'll be other contenders this time," Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., told Fox News Digital. "I've made no decisions about who I would support." "I think we're going to have a very, very, very messy and very big primary," Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., said. "It's going to be every Tom, Dick and Harry. And that's probably where it should be." "We're focused on 2026," said Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md. "We're going to win back the House and the Senate." She continued, "I love Kamala Harris. I have a very personal friendship and relationship. She's amazing. I think anybody who wants to run should. She's obviously very well qualified. We need to focus on '26."
news.summary: Kamala Harris allies questioned whether her respect within the Democratic Party translates to real support for a 2028 presidential election bid.

news.title: Trump's Approval Shift With This Voter Demo Will Make Your Jaw Drop
news.text:
President Donald Trump’s support among naturalized citizens has taken a shocking dive since he returned to the White House.

While immigrant voters showed up for Trump in historic numbers in 2024, his net approval rating with the demographic has plummeted a whopping 44 points since he was elected to his second term in office.

“It turns out that actions do, in fact, have consequences,” CNN’s Harry Enten said as he laid out the numbers for “News Central” on Tuesday morning.

Any gains Trump made with naturalized citizens in 2024 seem to have almost completely vaporized, with polling from the Pew Research Center showing support has tanked from -2 to -46 points in the past two years.

“Immigrant voters are waving ‘Adios amigos, goodbye’ to the president of the United States,” Enten told viewers.

Though CNN’s numbers guy said the economy and other issues were definitely factors, he had data showing how much Trump’s aggressive crackdown on immigration has shaped naturalized citizens’ opinions.

Citing polls where 60% of immigrant voters said they believed that Trump has gone too far on deportations, Enten said, “I think immigrant voters, just like other Americans, they thought they were signing up for one thing, and what they got was something very, very different, and they did not want what they see as the harshness of the Trump deportation policies.”

While Trump isn’t on the ballot this November, it appears that his unpopularity among immigrant voters will still have an effect on his fellow Republicans.

Naturalized citizens’ support for House Democrats sits at a net 22% compared to the 4% margin then-Vice President Kamala Harris had during her race against Trump.

“This is going to be a big part of the story,” Enten said. “If Republicans can’t hold onto them, it’s just another group that they haven’t been able to hold onto that Donald Trump made big gains with back in 2024.”

news.title: Meet the GOP Boogeymen
news.text:
Hasan Piker, a Twitch streamer with a niche yet growing following, is about as left as you can get. The GOP has done everything it can to elevate some of his most objectionable takes— about communism, about Israel. But he’s also really electrified some younger voters. One way was by showing up at the Republican midterm convention on a giant screen in his underwear.

Piker’s brother in liberalism is podcaster and YouTuber Adam Mockler. Like Piker, he’s been spending a lot of time talking to younger voters, getting them to debate him. He then attempts to translate what “the youths” are saying to the (presumably older) cable news viewer on networks like CNN.

Recently, the New York Times had the headline “Calls for Generational Change Don’t Resonate in Voting Booth,” which doesn’t square with what Piker and Mockler are hearing.

“I really disagree with that,” Mockler said. “Because we are seeing, right now, a massive shift in the power center of the Democratic Party towards younger voters, especially in the primaries.”

Nearly 20 percent of Congress is leaving their seats. Longtime folks like Sens. Gary Peters, Dick Durbin, and more are packing it in. Does this mean a new generation is going to take their place?

“The generational shift isn’t just about whether you’re an incumbent or a challenger,” Mockler said. “It can be communication on social media. It can be the way that you promise to use the power, once you actually have it, to change the lives of Americans. Or it can just be authenticity.”

On a recent episode of What Next, host Mary Harris spoke to Piker and Mockler about whether the November midterm could be one of generational change, and whether that change is actually here already. This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Mary Harris: I’m just going to take this back a little bit. I feel like ever since Joe Biden took to a debate stage and face-planted, Democrats in particular have been having this “generational change” conversation. And even though Kamala Harris eventually replaced Biden on the ballot, I feel this question—what if he passed the torch sooner?—is looming. And we’re about to have this midterm election, and it basically started off with the generational question. You had David Hogg, the activist survivor of the Marjory Stoneman Douglas school shooting, basically saying, “I want to primary people. We need a generational change.” 

It was interesting to me because even his message was a little bit muddied. In the beginning, he was explaining why he was supporting an 80-year-old incumbent in Illinois who eventually stepped out of her race. It shows to me how this generational change thing, you can’t define it by data points so well. But I do feel like what happened with Hogg was this moment where I realized how rocky things were going to be for the Dems. Are things better now? 

Adam Mockler: Forcibly so, yes. The voter base has changed the incentives that politicians follow, and the incentive is no longer to take money from special interest groups and do scripted, consultant-written television hits every single Sunday. Now it’s these more nimble, flexible videos, where you’re talking about the corruption of the system. I think the voters shifted the incentives of what politicians have to do in a campaign.

How do you see that? Are there particular races where you see this happening?

Hasan Piker: Yeah, absolutely. Melat Kiros in Denver unseated a long-term incumbent. Abdul El-Sayed is obviously the most nationally significant race. But Darializa Avila Chevalier unseated another incumbent, the head of the congressional Hispanic caucus, Adriano Espaillat. That’s a deep-blue district. But then Michigan is, quote-unquote, a purple state, or a swing state. I oppose that framing.

Piker: Michigan is never supposed to be a swing state. We turned it into a swing state with our ineptitude, with our incompetence, with NAFTA, and then also by not leaning into the populist rage that people were feeling. And that created a unique opportunity for the Republicans to basically farm that outrage and redirect it back to marginalized groups and generate a more convincing message that they were going to be the anti-war side—twice. Once against Hillary Clinton and also once against Kamala Harris, when it’s clear that they were never going to be anti-war. I mean, they are warmongers. They always start way more wars than even the Democrats do. This was very frustrating to observe from afar. That’s why I think Michigan is a blue state. It’s only turned into a swing state because we’ve missed.

I look at Abdul El-Sayed, and I actually see both the case for and against generational change. The New York Times just did a survey, and they showed that he has more support among young people than they’ve ever seen before—like 80-plus percent support from 18- to 29-year-olds, which is amazing, right? But that rests on them turning out. 

And then there was [Hasan Piker’s] involvement in the race, which has become a huge lightning rod because El-Sayed needs Jewish voters to turn out, and a lot of more conservative Jewish voters have looked at your involvement in that race and they’ve basically said, “You need to distance yourself from Hasan Piker.” Do you have any regrets, looking back at when were you out there? 

Piker: No, I do not have any. I did not have any concerns with my involvement whatsoever. I don’t think that it was the wrong thing to do. I think that we showed once again that we were able to defeat $70 million in outside expenditures.

But barely, right? The polls said that Hasan would perform way ahead, and he was much closer. I think that as we get closer, that’s where people are like, Oh, he’s making us nervous. 

Piker: Look, money in politics is obviously very important, right? It’s also very successful. I believe the stat is like 96 percent of the time, the side that has more money wins. And that makes sense. That means that you can set the narrative, you can set the agenda, you can disparage your opponent. Then your opponent has to spend a lot of money defending himself. Money plays a pretty formative role in these races.

Adam, I want to get you in here because I feel like another thing we’ve sort of danced around is what’s happening in Texas, where we have James Talarico. Here’s what I see when I look at that: I wonder if that race is about generational change or about a terrible Republican candidate on the other side. James Talarico is young, and he is pulling ahead of Ken Paxton, which is kind of amazing because Beto O’Rourke wasn’t doing that. But Paxton is a remarkably bad candidate. Even Donald Trump doesn’t seem to like him. Talk to me about this race. 

Mockler: It can be both/and. Obviously Talarico is a really strong candidate while Paxton is a very unique candidate. But it goes back to the framework I laid out at the beginning. You have to look at how Talarico is promising to use power once he gets it and how he’s communicating online. There’s this really viral video of Talarico calling Paxton’s cellphone number and asking him to debate him on Fox News, and Paxton doesn’t answer. He’s running from the debates. He’s openly admitting that he basically gave a plea deal to a [sex offender] named Adam Hoffman. He was impeached by his own party. All of this is true.

But on the other side of that, Talarico has very impressively used digital media, and look at his campaign promises. They are revolving around making the system work for the average voter. Many young people right now are skeptical that the system can even respond to us in a meaningful way, even if we did vote someone in. So, Talarico is proving that he will use this power in a very responsible way and to help people. A few weeks ago, Talarico went on Jimmy Kimmel’s show—that has 15 million views on YouTube. That’s using the new media, or at least the decentralized YouTube platform, to push your narrative. He makes short-form clips. He is a fighter who is bringing the fight to Ken Paxton, demanding that there’s some sort of debate. And overall, I think just taking money out of politics, advocating for a ban on gerrymandering, Supreme Court reform.

The GOP seems legitimately scared of Talarico. 

Mockler: Yeah, I know they are.

A lot of the candidates really don’t want to debate. 

Piker: Yeah. Mike Rogers ran away too. Mike Rogers ran away from the first debate. And he pointed to the fact that Roop Raj, who’s a very well-respected, credentialed reporter in Michigan, was biased in Abdul’s direction. I think it was a little bit racist for him to imply that. Because Roop Raj is brown, and they are obviously presenting Abdul as this, like, scary brown guy. Having said that, I think voters are seeing that. They’re not responding positively to that. And the cult, the base of power, that the Republicans have is shrinking every single day.

I do think we have to look at a couple of examples that argue against this idea that whatever happens in November is about generational change. I would start with Ohio, where we have Sherrod Brown, who’s in a good position to get back into the Senate. And he was there for years. And then you can look at North Carolina, where Thom Tillis is out, and Democrats nominated former Gov. Roy Cooper. That race is going so well for him that the GOP recently pulled money out of it. Those are two races where it is kind of about the same old Democratic Party. What do you say to that? 

Mockler: I think that Roy Cooper is a really strong candidate. If we back up, you can’t generalize with every single race that the nonincumbent is going to win. Different politicians have different coalitions. The coalition that Andy Beshear has in Kentucky is far different than the coalition that Zohran Mamdani built when he was winning in New York. Of course Ohio is going to look slightly different than Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed is likely to win. There are going to be exceptions to the rule, but oftentimes you see even these candidates leveraging social media and talking policy in a different way.

Piker: Look, Sherrod Brown is probably one of the more progressive Democrats, and he was a resilient force in Ohio politics for decades. And part of that was because of his uncompromising values. When it came to labor, he’s always been the guy backed by the state labor unions. And that is now giving him another unique opportunity to take a shot and to get back into office at a time when people are looking for that.

“Generational change” is people looking for real fighters. It is people that are demanding change in general. And yeah, if it works, it works. I’m not going to oppose more establishment-aligned Democrats winning their seats in places like North Carolina. I don’t want Republicans to be in office. I don’t want them to be in power. And I think that’s the beauty of democracy and is the beauty of this big-tent coalition that we’re trying to build here. There’s gonna be people like Zohran Mamdani, and then sometimes there’s going to be people like Roy Cooper as well.

Mockler: Or Liz Cheney, unfortunately. I mean, Hasan, every podcast or debate I go into over the past few months, people try to grill me on you, and they’re like, “Do you disavow Hasan Piker?” And it’s obviously not that simple. We disagree on certain things, but—

Do you disavow Hasan Piker? 

Mockler: In what regard? I mean—

Piker: I disavow myself all the time. Every day I wake up, I’m like, “I disavow myself.”

Mockler: Does Hasan have comments in 2019 that I disagree with? Yeah, sure. Even he disagrees with them. Does Hasan have policy positions that we can talk about in a rational way? Sure. But I keep getting asked about this. And I think the reality is: When we’re up against fascism, you have to look back at World War II. In World War II, they had such a broad coalition that you had, like, the communists, the socialists, you had the liberals, and you had even more Republican-leaning people all coalesced together to beat the fascists. So, if it’s Hasan Piker, if it’s Liz Cheney, whoever wants to stand up against this current administration, then they are welcome in the tent.

I love this kumbaya moment. 

Piker: We have to build allegiances. We don’t have the opportunity to just cast aside potential allies because of some twisted moral-purity attitude that we have.
news.summary: A generational change in politics is here. Just ask Hasan Piker and Adam Mockler.

news.title: White House blasts media coverage of Trump’s remark about Iran destroying LA and San Diego
news.text:
The White House blasted media coverage of President Donald Trump’s viral remarks about Iran destroying American cities, arguing that news outlets had taken his comments out of context.

At a rally in Nebraska on Monday, Trump discussed rising prices tied to the ongoing Iran war, calling them “a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe.”

“They could take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles; let them take out San Diego,” he said next, drawing cheers from the crowd. “This is a very small price to pay. And it’s gonna be over with very soon.”

The remarks quickly drew condemnation from Democrats and made headlines nationwide. The Los Angeles Times, for instance, ran the headline: “Trump suggests letting Iran 'take out' Los Angeles and San Diego at campaign rally.”

The White House responded by accusing the newspaper of misrepresenting Trump’s point.

“No, he didn't, you buffoons,” the White House Rapid Response account wrote on X in response to the Times’ article. “He was saying the U.S. is fighting to STOP Iran from having the ability to take out LA and San Diego with a nuclear weapon — which they would if they had the chance.”

White House Communications Director Steven Cheung echoed that defense.

“The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality,” he wrote on X. “He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped. America is safer because of the President.”

Trump also found an unlikely defender in CNN fact-checker Daniel Dale, who has spent years scrutinizing and debunking many of the president’s claims.

Dale challenged a post from Headquarters, an account linked to Kamala Harris, that shared a video of Trump with the caption: “Trump on Iran: Let 'em take out Los Angeles and San Diego, it's a small price to pay.”

“This isn’t a direct quote from Trump, and I very much don’t think it’s a correct paraphrase,” Dale wrote on X. “Trump has repeatedly argued that the consequences of the war, like higher gas prices, are a small price to pay compared to what an unchecked Iran could allegedly do.”

Dale added that Trump’s “rambling and incomplete fashion” of speaking made it difficult to discern his meaning. 

The president’s remarks drew swift condemnation Monday night from several top California Democrats.

“After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego,” California Governor Gavin Newsom wrote on social media. “He is deranged and dangerous.”

“The President of the United States suggested that a foreign government attack Los Angeles,” added Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass. “His statements against our city are dangerous and could potentially compromise our safety.”
news.summary: ‘The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality,’ White House Communications Director Steven Cheung wrote on social media
news.author: Brendan Rascius

news.title: Trump Attacks Female CNN Reporter With Oddly Specific Outfit Dig
news.text:
President Donald Trump hurled an insult at CNN’s senior White House correspondent Kristen Holmes once again this week, this time when she asked about his dwindling popularity among Latino voters. 

The terse exchange took place Monday outside of the White House when Holmes presented Trump with new polling information on the Republican Party’s chances in the midterms next month. 

The poll, published by NBC News/Telemundo earlier on Monday, found that only 27% of registered Latino voters ― often cited as a demographic critical to Trump’s 2024 victory over former Vice President Kamala Harris ― approve of the president’s performance.

When Holmes asked what Trump’s message to those voters would be, the president insisted he’s “doing great” before dismissing her and her outlet entirely. 

“You’re CNN, you’re fake news,” he replied. “My poll numbers are great, and all you have to do is look at the crowds we’re drawing, and every time I leave — that candidate will be losing — and by the time I leave, they’re winning.”

True to form, Trump then directed his words at Holmes. 

“CNN poll numbers are fake,” he snapped. “And your whole outfit is fake, and so are you.”

The insults aren’t particularly surprising given Trump’s relationship with CNN, which he temporarily banned from the White House last month. They’re also in line with his troubling history of attacks on prominent female journalists, including Holmes. 

In August, he lashed out at Holmes in the Oval Office, deeming her “very disrespectful” and a “loud, boisterous person” after she asked whether North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un had requested that the U.S. “scale back” its military exercises with South Korea. 

Later that day, Trump’s team tore into Holmes on social media over an inquiry regarding Sen. Jon Ossoff’s (D-Ga.) remarks about the president’s much-scrutinized relationship with White House aide Natalie Harp.

After deeming Holmes “a disgraceful, humiliating embarrassment” to her profession, the White House’s digital communications team wrote on X: “Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question. They will be sickened and embarrassed to have a parent be so callous and vindictive.”
news.author: Curtis M. Wong

news.title: Rasmussen Poll Gives Republicans Edge Among Hispanic Voters
news.text:
A nationwide Rasmussen Reports poll released Monday shows Hispanic voters favor Republicans by a 50 percent to 42 percent margin over Democrats. The poll also indicates a tightening battle for control of Congress, as the Democrats’ lead over Republicans decreased for the second week in a row, according to the company.

Overall, voters said if the election was held today 47 percent of likely voters would vote for the Democrat candidate, while 44 percent would vote for the Republican. Four percent of voters said another party’s candidate and just 4 percent were undecided.

Democrats led by eight points in mid-September in the national survey, particularly with independent voters. Republicans have closed the gap from an 18-point deficit to 9 points in the most recent poll.

Among Hispanic voters, Democrats held a slim 44 percent to 42 percent margin in mid-September, with the most recent survey giving Republicans the eight-point lead.

Republicans’ standing among Hispanic voters is significant given the corporate media establishment narrative of Hispanic voters fleeing the GOP.

In 2020, Joe Biden won Hispanic voters by 25 percentage points, and Hispanic voters supported Hillary Clinton by an even wider margin in 2016. But Trump drew nearly even with Kamala Harris among Hispanic voters, losing among them by only 3 points.

The Rasmussen survey of 1,794 U.S. Likely Voters was conducted on September 24 and 27-30, with a margin of error of +/- 2 percentage points and a 95 percent level of confidence.

news.title: Paramore’s Hayley Williams unleashes profanity-filled response after DHS tells her to ‘thank’ ICE
news.text:
Hayley Williams is not holding back when it comes to speaking out against Donald Trump’s administration.

After Williams said “f*** ICE” onstage during her concert in Chula Vista, California, in September, the outspoken Paramore lead singer sparked a response from the Department of Homeland Security.

“America is grateful all the time for our federal law enforcement officers who keep us safe,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement to Fox News. “We suggest Ms. Williams to thank them for their service, not belittle their sacrifice,” the agency’s statement said.

Williams, 37, then unleashed her response to the DHS’ statement in an Instagram Story post Monday: “And may I suggest all Nazi bitches suck on my fat d***.”

A DHS representative did not immediately return The Independent’s request for comment.

It has become standard for Williams to issue political messages like “f*** ICE” and “Free Palestine” from stage while on her solo tour, the Hayley Williams Show. 

Before playing her song “True Believer” — from her latest album Ego Death at a Bachelorette Party — the singer also typically makes a statement onstage that “the greatest threat to American democracy is Christian nationalism.”

Williams is a vocal critic of the president and Republican politicians. In 2024, she denounced Trump and his policies during Paramore’s performance at the iHeartRadio Music Festival in Los Angeles.

As the alternative rock band, who formed in 2004 in Tennessee, played their song “Big Man, Little Integrity,” Williams looked into the broadcast camera at the show and said: “Project 2025 is Donald Trump’s playbook for controlling and punishing women, poor people, people of color and the LGBTQ+ community.”

“It is time for all Americans to band together and to finally defeat the Trump agenda. And the only way to do that is by confronting him at the polls,” she said at the time, weeks before Trump defeated former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.

Williams concluded her message: “Do you want to live in a dictatorship?”

The “Ain’t It Fun” singer is in the company of several other musicians who have used their stages as platforms to speak out against the Trump administration. Superstars like Lady Gaga, Chappell Roan and Bruce Springsteen have all previously used their concerts to condemn Trump’s anti-immigration policies.

Earlier this year, rapper Cardi B got into an online feud with the DHS after she said she would “jump ICE” if the agency tried to detail fans at her concerts.
news.summary: ‘We suggest Ms. Williams to thank them for their service, not belittle their sacrifice,’ the DHS said

news.title: Biden conspicuously absent from campaign trail as Obama, Harris step up for midterm push
news.text: Former President Joe Biden has been largely absent from the campaign trail as Democrats fight to win back House and Senate majorities in November, even as former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris step up efforts to boost the party’s candidates. Biden, 83, has kept a limited public schedule while battling advanced, metastatic prostate cancer. He has endorsed candidates and is helping Democrats raise money, according to a source in Biden's political circle. But the former president has made few political appearances this year. The contrast is increasingly visible with four weeks to go until Election Day. Obama is cutting ads for Senate and gubernatorial candidates, helping the party fundraise and preparing to hit the trail during the closing stretch of the midterm campaign. Harris, the Democrats' 2024 presidential nominee, is also campaigning across key battleground states, including a recent stop in Michigan with Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. MIDTERM MATH: THE THREE FORCES THAT COULD STOP A DEMOCRATIC BLUE WAVE Biden has appeared at just a handful of political events this year. He spoke in February at a reception honoring his 2020 South Carolina primary victory, which propelled him toward the Democratic nomination and eventually the presidency. In June, he addressed a Maryland Democratic Party event. Longtime Democratic strategist Michael Ceraso told Fox News Digital that some in the party's elite and fundraising class are concerned that "if Biden were to be pushed out there in any sort of way for virtual or in-person opportunities, he could be a liability." Veteran Democratic strategist Maria Cardona had a different take, telling Fox News Digital, "there are still a ton of Americans who love Joe Biden." Biden did weigh in on a handful of Democratic primary showdowns this cycle. The former president endorsed former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms for governor. Bottoms, who later served as a senior advisor in the Biden administration, won the Georgia Democratic gubernatorial nomination. The former president also backed Dan Koh, another Biden administration veteran, who captured the Democratic nomination in Massachusetts' 6th Congressional District. HEAD HERE FOR THE LATEST FOX NEWS REPORTING ON FORMER PRESIDENT BIDEN Biden is also advocating on behalf of efforts to secure democracy. "American democracy begins and ends at the ballot box. There is no more important civic duty nor fundamental right to be defended," the former president wrote on social media last month, as he cast his ballot in his home state of Delaware's primary. "Voting defines our freedom and makes everything possible." But mostly, Biden has served as a foil for President Donald Trump, who Biden ousted from the White House in the 2020 election. Four years later, Biden ended his re-election bid after a disastrous debate performance against Trump in their 2024 rematch. Trump and fellow Republicans are repeatedly blaming Biden for high prices at the gas and diesel pumps, even though public opinion polls indicate most Americans now point fingers at Trump and his administration. Biden left the presidency with poor approval ratings, as he faced high inflation, foreign policy divides, and lingering questions about his ability to serve in office. He stood at 42% approval and 57% disapproval in January 2025, in the final Fox News poll during his White House tenure. Post-presidency, Biden held a 71% favorable rating among Democrats in a CNN poll conducted in May. But Biden's favorable rating among Democrats was 25 points lower than that of Obama. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB Meanwhile, some Democrats still blame him for Trump's 2024 re-election, arguing that Biden did not get out of the race in time to allow Harris to mount a successful campaign. Ceraso, a veteran of two presidential campaigns, pointed back to the 2024 election and told Fox News Digital that Biden left a "bad taste with some Democrats, especially within the in the party's elite and fundraising class." He added, "I do not think Biden has the same level of charisma as Vice President Harris and former President Obama, and if I'm organizing an event to get thousands of people to come out, I would not do that around Biden." Cardona, a Democratic National Committee member, said that Biden's health is stifling requests for campaign trail appearances.
