news.title: Map—Trump Approval Rating in Each Senate Swing State 4 Weeks Before Midterm
news.text: President Donald Trump’s approval rating is underwater in nearly all states with competitive Senate races in the 2026 midterm elections, according to the latest polling data from Civiqs. Trump’s approval rating will be a major factor in the midterm elections, as Democrats have sought to turn the elections into a referendum on the president’s popularity. Historically, when the president is unpopular, his party loses seats in the midterms. Democrats believe Trump’s approval rating hitting record lows in a series of recent polls could give them an opportunity to expand the battleground to compete in more conservative states. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate, so Democrats need to flip at least four seats to win control of the chamber, as Vice President JD Vance would serve as tiebreaker in an evenly divided Senate. Democrats are facing a tough map with few clear pickup opportunities. If they hold every seat they currently hold and pick up top targets in Maine and North Carolina, they would still need to win at least two seats in states that backed Trump by double digits in the 2024 election. A Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) spokesperson told Newsweek that Senate Republicans are “scrambling to defend deep red states and are desperately trying to change the subject from their scandal-plagued candidates and their toxic agenda of jacking up costs on everything from gas to groceries to health care.” Republican National Committee Press Secretary Natalie Baldassarre responded to polling in a statement to Newsweek. “President Trump and Republicans will continue barnstorming the country to highlight Democrats' extreme agenda, energize our base, and spend our resources to further our momentum in battleground races and drive Republicans to the polls,” she said. Newsweek also reached out to the Democratic National Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) for comment. What Is Donald Trump’s Approval Rating? Trump’s approval rating has reached record low points in several recent polls, creating a headache for Republicans in the final stretch of the midterms. His approval has fallen amid voters’ ongoing frustration with the economy, the cost of living and high gas prices soaring amid the unpopular war in Iran. Only 32 percent of Americans said they approved of Trump in the latest poll from Reuters and Ipsos, while 65 percent said they disapproved of his job performance. It surveyed 4,506 Americans from September 30 to October 5, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 1.5 percentage points. In a recent survey from YouGov and CBS News, 61 percent of Americans said they disapproved of Trump, while 39 percent approved. It was conducted among 2,166 adults from September 30 to October 2, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.5 percentage points. Trump’s net approval rating stood at -14 points in the latest Morning Consult poll, with 42 percent approving and 56 percent disapproving of his job performance. Its latest data was retrieved from a poll among registered voters ending the week of September 27. Trump has criticized polls showing his approval rating has fallen. On August 30, the president hit back at polls in a post on Truth Social. “THE FAKE POLLS USED BY OUR CROOKED MEDIA ARE OUT OF CONTROL, AND SOMETHING MUST BE DONE ABOUT IT. FCC TO THE RESCUE! President DJT,” he wrote. Donald Trump’s Approval Rating in Competitive Senate States Trump’s approval rating has important implications for the midterm elections. Democrats are targeting Senate seats in states like Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas, all of which backed Trump by double digits in the 2024 election, in addition to traditional swing states, in this year’s elections. Polls suggest those races are increasingly close, and Democrats have a plausible path to flipping the Senate majority. But many of these polls remain within the margin of error, meaning these races could go either way, and polling in some states has overestimated Democrats in the past. Here is a look at where Trump’s approval rating stands in these key races. Alaska Alaska has long been seen as a Republican stronghold, but things have shifted in the state. As Democrats gain ground in states like Anchorage and Fairbanks, Republicans’ statewide margins have narrowed from 31 points in 2000 to about 13 points in 2024. Democrats are optimistic about their nominee, former Representative Mary Peltola. She represented the state’s at-large congressional district from 2022 to 2025 and is the only Democrat to win statewide in the past few years. She is running against Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. Trump’s approval in Alaska stood at -16 points in the latest data from Civiqs, which provides a state-by-state look at their approval rating polling that has been conducted since Trump returned to office. The latest polls showed a close race. A survey from The New York Times and Siena University showed Peltola up 7 points, 50 percent to 43 percent. It surveyed 504 likely voters from September 24 to October 1, with a margin of error of plus or minus 5.1 percentage points. Peltola and Sullivan were locked in a statistical tie in the latest poll from Quantus Insights, which showed Sullivan with 46.1 percent and Peltola with 45.5 percent. It surveyed 737 voters from September 28 to 30 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. The Cook Political report classifies the Alaska Senate race as a toss-up. Georgia Trump carried Georgia by about 2 points in 2024, flipping it after former President Joe Biden narrowly won the Peach State in the 2020 election. Two years later, Trump’s approval rating has fallen to -25 points in the state, as Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff appears well-positioned in his reelection bid against Republican Representative Mike Collins. Georgia leaned toward Republicans for most of the 2000s and 2010s but emerged as a battleground due to growth around Atlanta and its blue-trending suburbs. Republicans have hoped that Trump’s victory two years ago could signal a potential for the state to be competitive again this year, but Ossoff has led polling. Ossoff led by 8 points in an InsiderAdvantage poll, 50 percent to 42 percent, that surveyed 1,200 likely voters from September 22 to 23. He also led a YouGov poll by 10 points, 52 percent to 42 percent. It surveyed 3,071 likely voters from September 15 to 18 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.7 percentage points. The Cook Political report classifies the Georgia Senate race as Likely Democratic. Iowa Iowa, once an important battleground state, has shifted rightward over the past decade, backing Trump by 13 points in 2024. But polls have shown his approval rating has fallen in the Hawkeye State, which stands to face impacts from his tariffs and high diesel prices due to its important agricultural base. His net approval rating stood at -19 points, according to Civiqs. The Senate race appears competitive as Republican Representative Ashley Hinson and state legislator Josh Turek are running to succeed retiring GOP Senator Joni Ernst, according to recent polling. Hinson was up 1 point in the latest poll from the Times, 48 percent to 47 percent. It surveyed 606 likely voters from September 22 to October 1 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.6 percentage points. Turek, however, led by 2 points in a Fox News poll, 49 percent to 47 percent. It surveyed 1,008 likely voters from September 24 to 28, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. The Cook Political report classifies the Iowa Senate race as a toss-up. Kansas Kansas is one of the more conservative states Democrats are hoping to compete in this year, as polls show a close race between Republican Senator Roger Marshall and Democrat Adam Hamilton. But Trump is still a bit more popular in Kansas, having a +2 approval rating, according to Civiqs. Democrats view Hamilton, a well-known pastor, as a particularly strong candidate in the Sunflower State against Marshall, who has faced criticism after The New York Times reported that he allegedly sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills. A poll from the Times showed a dead heat, with each candidate receiving 45 percent support. It surveyed 605 likely voters from September 22 to 30, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.6 percentage points. A recent poll from Emerson College also showed a statistical tie, with Hamilton receiving 45 percent and Marshall 43 percent. It surveyed 750 likely voters from September 15 to 16, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points. The Cook Political report classifies the Kansas Senate race as Lean Republican. Maine The Maine Senate race is expected to be one of the closest of the 2026 midterms, as Republican Senator Susan Collins is running against Democrat Troy Jackson, the former Maine Senate president. Trump has never been particularly popular in Maine. He lost the state all three times he ran for president, including by a 7-point margin in the 2024 election. His net approval was -33 points, according to Civiqs. Collins has been able to outrun other Republicans in the past due to her personal popularity and moderate image. But Democrats believe 2026 will be tougher for Collins due to Trump’s poor approval in the state. Democrats have sought to tie Collins to Trump, though the Republican senator has touted her votes against parts of his agenda such as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Democrats have also had a tumultuous campaign season in the Pine Tree State. Democrats initially nominated progressive Graham Platner as their nominee, but he withdrew from the race following sexual assault allegations he has denied. Jackson became the nominee after a Democratic convention over the summer. Collins, however, has faced scrutiny over a ProPublica report alleging her involvement in a pay-to-play scheme and a related probe by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, which her office has called "categorically false." Polls point to a close race. A Marist University poll gave Jackson a 4-point lead, 51 percent to 47 percent. It surveyed 1,505 registered voters from October 1 to 4, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points. The two candidates were tied at 50 percent in a YouGov poll, which surveyed 1,136 likely voters from September 23 to October 1, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.7 percentage points. The Cook Political report classifies the Maine Senate race as a toss-up. Michigan Michigan is a key battleground roughly evenly divided between Democrats and Republicans, backing Trump by fewer than 2 points in 2024. Trump’s approval stood at -26 points in Civiqs as the race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Representative Mike Rogers heats up. Democrats have hoped the national environment would benefit them in swing states like Michigan, but polls have suggested the race is close. Republicans hope to cast El-Sayed, a progressive endorsed by Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders and New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, as too far left for a more moderate state. Democrats have overall lost ground in the state over the past decade. While it once easily backed Obama, it has become much more competitive as Republicans win over white, rural voters. Democrats have, however, made up for those losses by gaining ground in Detroit suburbs and Western Michigan. El-Sayed led by 4 points in a recent survey from Mitchell Research & Communications, 45.6 percent to 41.4 percent. It polled 682 likely voters on October 1, 2026, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points. However, a Fox News poll showed an even closer race, giving El-Sayed just a single-point lead, 50 percent to 49 percent. It was conducted by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research from September 24 to 28 among 1,028 likely voters. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. The Cook Political report classifies the Michigan Senate race as a toss-up. Minnesota Trump lost Minnesota by about 4 points in 2024, so it’s another state where Democrats have hoped it would not be competitive. Trump is unpopular in the state, having a -34 point approval rating, per Civiqs. But polls have pointed to a closer-than-expected race between Democratic Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan and Republican Michele Tafoya. Flanagan held a single-point lead in a recent InsiderAdvantage poll, 46 percent to 45 percent, which surveyed 1,200 likely voters from September 28 to 29, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.95 percentage points. Meanwhile, the two candidates were tied in a SurveyUSA poll sponsored by KSTP-TV, each receiving 42 percent of the vote. It surveyed 654 likely voters from September 9 to 14, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. Immigration is a major flash point in the Minnesota Senate race. Republicans have sought to tie Flanagan to a fraud scandal that brought scrutiny toward Governor Tim Walz’s administration. The scandal centered around the Feeding Our Future nonprofit, which was implicated in a $250 million COVID-era scheme involving fraudulent claims for child nutrition programs. The Justice Department’s probe, which began under the Biden administration, has led to dozens of indictments. In light of the scandal, Minnesota became the epicenter of the Trump administration’s ramped-up immigration enforcement earlier this year. Two American citizens, Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti, were fatally shot by federal immigration officers in January amid protests in Minneapolis, fueling anger over the White House's hard-line approach to immigration and border security. The Cook Political report classifies the Minnesota Senate race as a Likely Democratic. Nebraska Trump easily carried Nebraska by more than 20 points in 2024, so it’s not ordinarily a seat for which Democrats would make a play. But there is no Democrat on the ballot in November. Instead, the race is between Republican Senator Pete Ricketts and independent Dan Osborn. Trump’s approval is underwater in Nebraska, but by a closer margin than in other states, at -4 points. But polls still show a close race, and Trump has campaigned in the state with Ricketts. Ricketts was up by 5 points in the latest co/efficient poll, 45 percent to 40 percent. It surveyed 1,113 likely voters from September 28 to 30 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.92 percentage points. A SurveyUSA poll gave Osborn a 4-point lead, 46 percent to 42 percent, with 4 percent preferring another candidate and 7 percent being undecided. It surveyed 503 likely voters September 8-13. The Cook Political report classifies the Nebraska Senate race as Likely Republican. New Hampshire Republicans view the New Hampshire Senate race as a rare pickup opportunity this year, despite the state backing former Vice President Kamala Harris by about 3 points in 2024. Trump’s approval rating is also poor in the state, standing at -35 points, according to Civiqs. Democratic Representative Chris Pappas and Republican former Senator John Sununu are running to succeed Senator Jeanne Shaheen, a Democrat, in the Granite State. Democrats believe the national environment will help carry Pappas across the finish line, but Sununu is seen as a strong candidate, having formerly held this seat and being part of a popular political family. Pappas led Sununu by 5 points in a recent poll from The New York Times and Siena University, 50 percent to 45 percent. It surveyed 613 likely voters from September 15 to 22, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.8 percentage points. A poll from the University of New Hampshire gave Pappas an 8-point lead, 50 percent to 42 percent, among likely voters. It was conducted from September 17 to 21, among 1,392 likely voters. The Cook Political report classifies the New Hampshire Senate race as a toss-up. North Carolina Trump won North Carolina by 3 points in 2024, so his slim victory in the state was going to leave it as a contested state in this year’s midterms, even though Democrats last won a Senate race in the Tar Heel State in 2008. Trump’s approval rating stood at -18 points in the state, according to Civiqs. Democratic former Governor Roy Cooper is running against Republican Michael Whatley, the former chair of the Republican National Committee. Republican Senator Thom Tillis is retiring at the end of the current term. Polls have given Cooper a lead over Whatley. A recent AAR poll showed Cooper up by 11 points, 53 percent to 42 percent. It was conducted by Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research from September 17 to 20. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points and surveyed 1115 likely voters. Cooper was also up 5 points, 48 percent to 43 percent, in a recent survey from Quantus Insights, which surveyed 686 likely voters from September 21 to September 22. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.2 percentage points. The Cook Political report classifies the North Carolina Senate race as Lean Democratic. Ohio Once a battleground that backed former President Barack Obama in 2008 and 2012, Ohio has shifted rightward over the past decade, electing Trump in all three of his presidential runs. Trump’s approval was -18 points, according to Civiqs. The special election is being held to finish Vance's term. Senator Jon Husted, a Republican, was appointed to fill the vacancy by Governor Mike DeWine and is facing a challenge from former Senator Sherrod Brown, who lost reelection in 2024 but won reelection in 2018. Brown has held narrow leads in recent polling. He led by 3 points in a poll from the Times, 49 percent to 46 percent. It polled 616 likely voters from September 22 to October 1 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.5 percentage points. A Suffolk University poll also gave Brown a 3-point lead, 47 percent to 44 percent. It surveyed 500 likely voters from September 23 to 27, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. The Cook Political report classifies the Ohio Senate race as a toss-up. South Carolina A series of polls have pointed to a closer-than-expected race in South Carolina, which backed President Donald Trump by nearly 18 points in the 2024 presidential election. His approval has slipped to -9 points in the state, according to Civiqs. The race is between Senator Darline Graham, who was appointed to the seat following the death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, and Democrat Annie Andrews, a doctor who ran for Congress in 2022. A recent poll from InsiderAdvantage gave Graham only a single-point lead, 46 percent to 45 percent, within the margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. The survey was conducted from September 28 to 29, 2026. A recent poll from Trafalgar Group, a Republican pollster, also showed her with a single-point lead, 43 percent to 42 percent, which falls within its margin of error of 2.9 points. It surveyed 1,087 likely voters from September 23 to 25. The Cook Political report classifies the South Carolina Senate race as Likely Republican. Texas Texas, which has been a Republican stronghold for decades, has emerged as part of the battleground in this year’s election. Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton unseated Senator John Cornyn in the GOP primary and is set to face Democratic state Representative James Talarico in November. Paxton, who has faced a series of scandals, is viewed as particularly vulnerable despite GOP investment to boost his polling. Democrats are optimistic about the latest polling data in Texas, where they have hoped to flip but fallen short in the past. According to Civiqs, Trump’s approval is 20 points underwater in the Lone Star State. The latest polls from the Times and Fox News give Talarico an edge. Talarico led by 6 points, 51 percent to 45 percent, in the Times poll and by 2 points, 51 percent to 49 percent, in the Fox News poll. The Times poll surveyed 615 likely voters from September 21 to 30 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.5 percentage points. The Fox News poll surveyed 881 likely voters from September 24 to 28 with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. The Cook Political report classifies the Texas Senate race as a toss-up. Democrats’ Chances of Flipping the Senate Amid Trump Approval Rating Collapse Democrats have emerged as favorites to flip control of the Senate in prediction markets. On Kalshi, Democrats had a 64 percent chance of winning a majority on Tuesday, a shift from one month earlier when Republicans had a 53 percent chance of doing so. Democrats also had a 65 percent chance of flipping the Senate on Polymarket, up from a 52 percent chance one month earlier. Prediction markets let traders buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real-money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always predict the future accurately. What Happens Next Trump’s approval rating will remain closely watched as an important gauge of the electorate’s mood ahead of the November 3 elections. His approval could be shaped by issues like the economy and cost of living over the coming weeks, as candidates continue to make their final pitches to voters ahead of the midterms. news.summary: Donald Trump's approval rating is underwater in nearly every state with a competitive Senate race in the 2026 midterm elections.
news.author: Andrew Stanton

news.title: CNN Fact-Checker Actually Defends Trump Over 'Let 'Em Take Out' LA Remarks
news.text:
CNN fact-checker Daniel Dale often spends his days pointing out Donald Trump’s lies, falsehoods, exaggerations and basic untruths.

So it was a bit of a surprise that Dale took to social media Tuesday to defend the president against an account associated with Democrats.

During a Monday night rally in Nebraska, the president attempted to justify the high costs and inflation associated with the Iran war by suggesting a grim alternative.

“Remember, with the war, it’s just artificial. It’s a little bit high. It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. They could take out a city. Let ’em take out Los Angeles. Let ’em take out San Diego.”

White House staffers insist Trump wasn’t saying he wanted Iran to attack the U.S. but that he wants to prevent Tehran from having the ability to do so.

Trump’s fiery comments attracted attention, and @HQNewsNow, an account associated with former Vice President Kamala Harris, posted a clip of his comments captioned, “Trump on Iran: Let ’em take out Los Angeles and San Diego, it’s a small price to pay.” 

Although the clip contained the complete remarks, Dale objected to the caption in a lengthy social media post, saying, “This isn’t a direct quote from Trump, and I very much don’t think it’s a correct paraphrase.”

He also noted that Trump has “repeatedly argued that the consequences of the war, like higher gas prices, are a small price to pay compared to what an unchecked Iran could allegedly do.”

He suggested the reason people think Trump was saying he wanted Iran to attack Los Angeles and San Diego is that “you kinda have to be steeped in TrumpRallySpeak to know what he was saying last night.”

Dale then noted that while it’s fair to say “it’s inappropriate” for a president “to casually float the possibility of a city being wiped out,” he insisted “the context exists and is important.”
news.author: David Moye

news.title: Potential 2028 Democratic contenders set to discuss party’s future at post-midterms meeting
news.text: A group of potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidates is heading to Denver days after the midterms to discuss the party’s future, in one of the party’s first major gatherings following the election.Attendees will include former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and former US Ambassador to Japan Rahm Emanuel, as well as Sens. Ruben Gallego of Arizona, Chris Murphy of Connecticut, Raphael Warnock of Georgia and Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, according to an initial lineup shared first with CNN. The group of speakers also includes Govs. Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey and Abigail Spanberger of Virginia, plus several additional members of Congress.The “What’s Next” summit is being hosted from November 12-14 by Majority Democrats, an organization that launched last year to help Democrats win in more places.RELATED STORY | New midterm polling gives Democrats an edge in battleground statesIn staging the event less than two weeks after the midterms, where Democrats hope to retake the Senate and the House, the group is looking to move quickly to outline the lessons learned from the election that could be instructive going forward, including in the next White House race.“This isn’t a policy conference nor a talk shop on tactics,” said Massachusetts Rep. Jake Auchincloss, chair of Majority Democrats, in a statement. “What’s Next is timed for a unique moment after the midterms and before the presidential to debate a vision for the Democratic Party. Politicians who believe they have that vision should be on that stage.”Organizers chose Denver partly because it is one of the cities under consideration to host the 2028 Democratic National Convention.The initial lineup also includes top party strategists such as David Axelrod, former senior adviser to President Barack Obama and a chief political analyst at CNN; Quentin Fulks, former principal deputy campaign manager for Kamala Harris in 2024; and Morris Katz, adviser to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Trump claims Iran is waiting until after midterm elections to strike dealMajority Democrats is not the only organization holding an event in the immediate aftermath of the midterms in a bid to shape the party’s future. news.title: Is Obama the Democrats’ Silver Bullet or Break-Glass Option for the Midterms?
news.text:
That question came up Monday on CNN's NewsNight, where Elie Honig reported that Obama will campaign later this month with Michigan Democrat Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. Obama has also recorded two dozen ads for the party's Senate and gubernatorial candidates, with more trail appearances to come. Honig then turned to Scott Jennings and asked whether Republicans "welcome or fear Barack Obama's involvement in these midterms."

"Well, neither, because it's expected," Jennings said. "He campaigns in every election. He's the most partisan, ate up with politics ex-president we've ever had. I expect him to show up in every race, in every jurisdiction of the country. He can't stand it. He has to be involved in politics all the time."

He's right. Republicans aren't fearing Obama's involvement, and for starters, it was inevitable that he'd jump in. Nobody at the RNC is losing control over their bowels because Barack Obama is once again clamoring for the spotlight in an election year.

What should amuse Republicans is where he's going. Obama is going to stump for El-Sayed in Detroit, a Democrat stronghold if one ever existed. A confident party doesn't spend its biggest name on a city it should carry in its sleep. Sending Obama into Detroit is a de facto acknowledgment that Democrats are worried about their own base turning out.

Jennings saw the same thing, and he pointed to El-Sayed's bruising primary against the more moderate Haley Stevens.

"What it tells me, though, is that all this Democratic confidence you hear out there about El-Sayed is a little misplaced because I don't think Obama would be going there if they were so confident about it," he said.

"He has significant trouble with African-American voters in the Democratic primary," Jennings added about El-Sayed. "He has not shored up that support in Michigan. They need Obama to try to do that. I'm not sure it's going to be the total answer, but it's not really a surprising development to me."

"Obama campaigns in every election. He's the most partisan ate up with politics ex-President we've ever had." "All this Democrat confidence about El-Sayed is misplaced, Obama wouldn't be going there if they were confident." Scott Jennings is right. Democrats are panicking. https://t.co/FhMzWqOkBk— Thomas Hern (@ThomasMHern) October 6, 2026

So Obama's involvement looks less like a show of strength and more like an admission that Democrats have a problem. The real question is whether it will work. And we don't have to look far back to see that Obama's ability to deliver for his party isn't as strong as it used to be.

Consider the final weeks of 2024, when Obama barnstormed the battlegrounds for Kamala Harris. He campaigned for her in Pennsylvania and dropped by a campaign field office in Pittsburgh. He held a rally at a Nevada high school. He rallied with Tim Walz at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. He joined Kamala, Bruce Springsteen, and Tyler Perry at a huge rally in Georgia, their first joint campaign appearance. In late October, he campaigned in Michigan, including a Detroit event with her campaign. With the exception of Georgia, Obama carried every one of those states when he ran for president. These were his states and his voters.

Yet Kamala lost all of them.

That's why Honig's question misses the point. Asking whether Republicans fear Obama assumes his involvement moves votes. The better question is whether it helps Democrats at all. If he couldn't win a single swing state for Kamala in 2024, what good will he be in 2026?
news.author: Matt Margolis

news.title: New poll shows ban on trans athletes in girls' sports could pass in Washington... as activists claim silent support ahead of historic vote
news.text:
Washington state is set to vote on barring transgender athletes from competing in women's sports - with activists increasingly confident that the ban will pass. 

The state will vote on Initiative 638 on November 3, which, if passed, would ban biological males from competing in girls' K-12 sports.

It took hundreds of thousands of signatures from across Washington to get the measure on the ballot. 

And, despite being an overwhelmingly liberal state, there is optimism among activists that the initiative could pass. 

Tentative new local polling has reportedly shown that Washington voters will cast their ballots in favor of passing the ban. 

Polling conducted by Let's Go Washington, a conservative-backed political action committee that advocated for the proposed ban, shows 56 percent of the vote going in favor of the ban in November, according to KUOW. 

'People are with us, and they don't wanna say it out loud,' Hallie Herzberg, a spokesperson for Let's Go Washington, told the outlet. 'They don't want to be villainized for it. They will support us, and they will stand up for girls, but they will do it in the safety of their own ballot.' 

Meanwhile, nationally 66 percent of Americans are said to support policies that force trans athletes to play on sports teams that 'match their sex at birth,' according to polling that the Pew Research Center published last year.

Voters trend towards supporting banning trans athletes from competing with cisgender girls after they read the language used to describe the initiative as it will appear on the November ballot, according to Andrew Villeneuve, the founder of Northwest Progressive Institute, which has conducted some additional polling on the matter. 

However, Democrats have conducted limited polling on the matter with party spokesperson Stephen Reed telling KUOW that, 'This is not a slam dunk like some folks think it might be.' 

27 states have already passed policies that separate biological males from competing in women's sports in K-12. However, all of those policies were passed by state legislature rather than the popular vote. 

Therefore, should Washington pass the initiative in November, it would become the first state to enact the policy through voter approval, according to Fox News. 

Furthermore, it would also become the first state that Donald Trump lost to Kamala Harris in the 2024 election to adopt such a policy. 

The President signed an executive order in February 2025 aimed at keeping trans athletes out of girls' and women's sports. 

Washington outright rejected the order with the state's Superintendent Chris Reykdal immediately speaking out against the policy. 

Reykdal said in a statement that the order tried to force schools to 'discriminate against trans female athletes' in exchange for federal funds, and that it sought to 'restrict transgender girls from participating in girls' sports with their peers.' 

He called the order unlawful, saying it contradicted the Washington Law Against Discrimination and state school rules. He added: 'Our state law prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity, and we will not back down from that.' 

Meanwhile, several female athletes have spoken out ahead of the vote with one high school student filing an appeal to the Supreme Court. 

Kallie Keeler, a high school girls wrestler, filed for an injunction, seeking that she be allowed to wrestle this season without being matched against a male, or that her mother receive notice so she can opt out without penalty. 

Keeler alleges she was sexually assaulted by a male opponent during a girls' match in December and was not told he was male beforehand.

However, Washington's high school athletics association and the state superintendent have stood firm ahead of November's vote, saying they will keep letting students compete by gender identity while the SCOTUS application is pending. 

The Washington Office of Superintendent of Public Instruction (OSPI), which enforces state law on extracurricular activities, stood by the state's current, pre-vote policy. 

'While OSPI does not oversee athletics in our state, our office is responsible for communicating, upholding, and enforcing the law, including in student athletics and extracurricular activities,' the superintendent's office told OutKick. 

'OSPI will continue to uphold Washington's current law unless or until the law changes. OSPI does not have any non-privileged statement, board notice, or guidance that we have issued to schools or staff regarding this appeal.
news.summary: Washington state will vote on Initiative 638 on November 3, which, if passed, would ban biological males from competing in girls' K-12 sports.

news.title: CNN Data Guru Reveals Trump’s 44-Point Drop Disaster
news.text:
CNN’s resident numbers guru has laid out just how badly President Donald Trump is hemorrhaging with immigrant voters who helped power his 2024 comeback. 

The network’s data reporter Harry Enten walked viewers through the damage live on Tuesday morning on News Central, after anchor Kate Bolduan noted that naturalized citizens casting ballots helped Trump win the White House in 2024 but that the latest polls show he has lost most of their support.

In late 2024, he noted, Trump’s net approval among immigrant voters was “pretty gosh darn good for a Republican president.” Those gains, Enten said, “are basically collapsing.”

“It turns out that actions do in fact have consequences,” he said.

The biggest consequence, Enten argued, is Trump’s deportation push. Back in 2024, voters trusted Trump more than Kamala Harris on immigration policy by four points. Now, Enten said, 60 percent of immigrant voters say Trump has gone too far on deportations. He said they thought they were “signing up for one thing and what they got was something very, very different.”

“They did not want what they see as the harshness of the Trump deportation policies,” Enten said. 

He added that the cost of living is also driving the slide, and that Trump is now back at levels “he might have been used to seeing during term number one.”

The slide could hurt Republicans well beyond the White House. “President Trump, as much as he wishes, is not on the ballot in a month,” Enten said. “Who is on the ballot is Republicans running for Congress.”

Among immigrant voters, Democrats now lead by 22 points on the generic congressional ballot, Enten said, a shift of 18 points away from the Republican Party. In 2024, Trump lost the group to Harris by only four points, so the Democratic lead is now more than five times as big.

Immigrants make up about 10 percent of voters, Enten said, “a significant chunk.” If Republicans can’t keep them, he said, “it’s just yet another group that they haven’t been able to hold onto that Donald Trump made big gains with back in 2024.”
news.summary:
Kevin Dietsch/Getty ImagesCNN’s resident numbers guru has laid out just how badly President Donald Trump is hemorrhaging with immigrant voters who helped power his 2024 comeback. 

The network’s data reporter Harry Enten walked viewers through the damage live on Tuesday morning on News Central, after anchor Kate Bolduan noted that naturalized citizens casting ballots helped Trump win the White House in 2024 but that the latest polls show he has lost most of their support.

“Look at this now. Minus 46 points falling through the floor. My goodness gracious, that’s a shift of 44 points away from the President of the United States amongst a group that he did historically well with for a Republican presidential candidate. Voters are waving adios amigos goodbye to the President of the United States,” Enten said.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

news.title: Alaska Senate Seat Leans Democratic for First Time in 18 Years
news.text: For the first time in almost 20 years, Alaska appears to be leaning toward electing a Democratic Party candidate to the United States Senate, after a key indicator moved the state from a toss-up. Sabato's Crystal Ball, based out of the University of Virginia's Center for Politics, moved the Alaska race to "Leans Democratic" from its previous "toss-up" ranking, while demoting South Carolina from a safe Republican seat to a likely one. The Alaska shift is notable as the last time the state looked likely to vote blue was in 2008, when Democrat Mark Begich won after incumbent GOP Senator Todd Stevens was indicted on seven felony counts before Election Day. Tuesday's shift reflects current Democratic candidate Mary Peltola's growing lead in recent polling, despite incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan's appearances alongside President Donald Trump for a major investment announcement for the state, and a rally with Vice President JD Vance on Monday. "Alaska is impacted by the good Democratic environment just like so many other states are, and Peltola is a strong challenger," Kyle Kondik, the managing editor of Sabato’s Crystal Ball, told Newsweek. "Additionally, Alaska has a top-four, ranked choice voting system that wasn't in place in 2020, and the structure of the ballot (Peltola is the only Democrat) likely aids her as well." During the rally Monday night, Vance touted Sullivan's record, while accusing Democrats of being "obsessed" with Alaska. "AOC and Kamala Harris and the rest of them. They see the Last Frontier as their last best hope to take America in a far-left direction, to impeach Donald Trump, to turn off the energy projects that we're building all across this state, and to throttle this state and this country's incredible progress," Vance said. While Sullivan's good relationship with Trump appeared to boost his reelection campaign in 2020, souring approval ratings for the president in recent months could now be a drag on the incumbent's chances of a third term. Newsweek reached out to the Peltola and Sullivan campaigns for comment Tuesday morning via email. This is a breaking news story. Updates to follow. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Sam Wilson.
news.summary: The shift comes as Democrat Mary Peltola extends her poll lead, despite White House efforts to boost Senator Dan Sullivan.

news.title: Why polls keep getting it wrong on Brazil's right
news.text:
Once again, Brazilian pollsters missed the mark in a first-round election on Sunday, joining many around the world who have struggled to gauge support for the right from voters who can be cagey about their choices.

"I am very pleased because many polling institutes had us trailing," right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro said after edging past President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday's election.

He is now a firm favourite as the race goes to a run-off vote on October 25.

The son of far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro, the opposition candidate secured nearly 47 percent of the vote, compared to Lula's 45 percent.

The Datafolha pollster had Lula three percentage points ahead of his rival in the first round, while Quaest showed a one-point lead for Lula.

Survey firms have been blindsided in other countries too.

In the United States, some polls wrongly predicted a victory for Democrat Kamala Harris over Donald Trump in the 2024 elections.

In Latin America, polls also failed to anticipate the strong showing of libertarian firebrand Javier Milei in Argentina or conservative Rodrigo Paz in Bolivia.

Right-wing and far-right forces in Europe have also bucked predictions.

In many cases, these parties have positioned themselves as anti-establishment options and capitalize on social discontent. 

"There is the phenomenon of the 'shy vote' phenomenon, where voters don't choose a candidate on their merits, but because they dislike the other options," Marco Carvalho Teixeira, a political scientist at the Getúlio Vargas Foundation, told AFP.

Such voters will not disclose their choice to pollsters.

Brazil's first-round election also featured "high volatility" among undecided voters right up to the end of the campaign, making predictions difficult, says Carvalho Teixeira. 

James Bosworth, a consultant and author of the Latin American Risk Report, a political risk newsletter, said pollsters overestimated the support of third-party candidates who garnered only eight percent of the vote on Sunday.

He said some voters who had expressed support for one of the smaller candidates "voted strategically" and opted for one of the leading candidates in a bid to make their vote count – which Bolsonaro had pushed hard for on the campaign trail.

Nevertheless, the polling error was smaller this year than in the first round of elections in 2022 when polls gave Lula a 10-point advantage over Jair Bolsonaro. He came first by only five.

"In the last four elections, the Brazilian right performed three to four percent better than the polls predicted," Bolsonaro's campaign manager, Senator Rogerio Marinho, told AFP ahead of the vote.



by Facundo Fernández Barrio, AFP
news.summary: Pollsters across the world have struggled to gauge support for the right from voters who can be cagey about their choices. Brazil's election, last Sunday, was no different. Leer más

news.title: The one GOP incumbent who’s poised to defy the odds in midterms bloodbath
news.text:
The midterm election is less than a month away. And all signs point to a bloodbath for President Donald Trump and the Republican Party. The generic congressional ballot, which measures whether voters will pick a generic Democrat or Republican for Congress, shows Democrats have a nine-point lead. 

On an individual level, Democrats have wide leads in swing states like Georgia and North Carolina. And Trump’s gamble to replace the genteel Republican incumbent Sen. John Cornyn with MAGA Attorney General Ken Paxton seems to be blowing up in his face, as Democrat James Talarico leads in polling and fundraising. Vice President JD Vance had to be sent to Alaska Monday, which Trump won by 13 points, to campaign for Dan Sullivan. 

Republicans’ resources will now be stretched thin as they have to play defense not only in the traditional swing states, but even in ruby-red states like Kansas, Iowa and Nebraska. But ironically, even if Democrats massacre Republicans at the polls, they might not get their one prized possession: unseating Sen. Susan Collins in Maine.

On Tuesday night, she will square off in a debate against her Democratic opponent, former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson. By all measures, this should be the year that the five-term incumbent Republican goes down. Kamala Harris won Maine by about seven points. 

The state has a Democratic governor and legislature. Earlier this year, an Immigration and Customs officer in Biddeford shot and killed Joan Sebastian Guerrero. Democrats like Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have tried to pin the death on Collins since she voted for increased funding for ICE earlier this year, though Collins argues she put in place body cameras for ICE. 

But polling shows Collins is still in the hunt. A CBS poll showed that she is in a dead heat with Jackson. But other polls show a more difficult race for the challenger. And it might mean that Maine does not live up to its politics motto: “As Maine goes, so goes the nation.” 

Two weeks ago, a New York Times/Siena University poll showed Collins with a three-point lead. 

On the surface, it looks fairly easy to blame this on the debacle that was the Democratic Primary, wherein insurgent candidate Graham Platner won before he ultimately dropped out after a report in Politico that he allegedly sexually assaulted an ex-partner, which he denied. The fact Jackson campaigned heavily with Platner when Jackson ran for governor made it fairly easy for Republicans to tie the two together. 

A look under the hood seems to shows that’s only part of the story. Democrats hope to tie Collins, who has portrayed herself as a moderate New England Republican, closer to Trump this cycle, especially after she voted to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court.

But she still enjoys some crossover support. The Times/Siena poll showed that 44 percent of women still support Collins. Compare that with The Times/Siena Michigan’s Senate race, where only 39 percent of women support Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers. The same holds true for The Times/Siena poll in Kansas, where 40 percent of women support incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall. 

Collins also still has support among a significant slice of Democrats, with 13 percent of self-identified Democrats saying if the election were held today, they’d pick Collins. By contrast, in Michigan, 95 percent of Democrats said they would support Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed. The same amount of Democrats in Texas would vote for Talarico.

Collins also leads Jackson 51 percent to 45 percent with voters identified as “other.” In Kansas, Hamilton has 55 percent of voters with that identification. In Michigan, El-Sayed and Rogers are about dead-even with independents, with 46 percent for El-Sayed and 45 percent.

This support can really only come with years of support Collins has cultivated from being a senator since 1996. As chairwoman of the Senate Appropriations Committee, she regularly touts the millions of dollars she brings back to a largely rural state like Maine and the fact she is an independent senator. 

Collins also bolstered her independent image by voting to convict Trump after January 6, opposing the confirmation of Pete Hegseth as Defense secretary, the confirmation of Todd Blanche as attorney general and the passage of the One, Buig Beautiful Bill. The fact that Collins is probably the only Republican who can win that seat is likely why Trump has largely refrained from criticizing her.

And the chances are that Collins might have more support than even the polls are showing. In 2020, a host of polls had Collins down for the count, only for her to shock everyone and win by almost 8.6 points despite Joe Biden winning the state by about 9 points.

There are significant differences between then and now, though. Collins no longer has the cache of being seen as a pro-abortion rights Republican given the Supreme Court’s Dobbs v Jackson decision in 2022 that killed the constitutional right to an abortion. And she’s voted more in line with Trump this go-around. 

Still, if she pulls off a victory, don’t be entirely surprised that she has pulled one last rabbit out of her hat.
news.summary: Susan Collins might be the one Republican who survives a GOP electoral bloodbath, Eric Garcia writes, defying the old saw, 'As goes Maine, so goes the nation'
news.author: Eric Garcia

news.title: Why older lawmakers may wait too long to step aside
news.text:
U.S. Sen. Ed Markey is 80 and has served in Congress for half a century. His Democratic primary challenger in Massachusetts, U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton, is 47 and made generational change a centerpiece of his campaign. Markey won the Sept. 1, 2026, primary anyway by nearly 30 percentage points.

He’s not the only octogenarian to prevail in a competitive primary in 2026. Eleven won their primaries and are on the ballot for the 2026 midterm elections. The oldest primary winner was Sen. Jim Risch of Idaho, an 83-year-old Republican.

It seems to be an issue both major political parties agree on: For many candidates, age is just a number, even when it starts with an 8 or a 9.

My colleagues and I study succession in family-run businesses and other occupations where leadership, identity and longevity can become deeply intertwined. Whether someone is in charge of a company or is a lawmaker, their work does not only keep them busy. It provides status, an identity and a sense of mission. Letting go means giving up more than a job. 

When business leaders or politicians linger for too long, it can be costly for their companies or constituents because potential successors may become frustrated by waiting and decide to move on.

When any kind of leader remains in their role for decades, underlying reasons can range from a genuine love for what they do to not knowing what they will do – or who they will be – once they leave. However, waiting too long can mean they’ll have to hand off their responsibilities in crisis mode. 

In family businesses, my research team found, the people closest to their leaders – including relatives, employees and longtime supporters – may go quiet rather than press the issue. 

This dynamic is not limited to the business world. It also applies to many of the older members of Congress.

A closer look at the large numbers of legislators who continue to serve during their golden years reflects two trends.

First, many are elected for the first time when they’re middle-aged. New House members were about 50 years old and new senators around 55 in 2025.

Second, although the median age of House lawmakers is now about 60, and 66 in the Senate, there’s a small group of long-serving members who remain in office into and past their 80s and keep running for reelection.

Seeing the advantages of ‘not yet’

Every lawmaker can have a reason to say “not yet.” So can their staff members, who may be loyal to them and their missions and professionally invested in the work they have built together.

Political parties value the electoral advantages of incumbents, while constituents may value the seniority, relationships and influence that come with having spent decades serving in Congress. And incumbents can sincerely believe important work remains unfinished.

However, unusually prolonged service in any position increases the possibility that illness, cognitive decline or death will lead to an unplanned and probably rocky transition.

What’s more, when politicians serve into their late 70s, 80s or beyond, they are breaking with ordinary employment patterns.

The typical American retires in their early 60s, with two-thirds of U.S. workers exiting the labor force before their 65th birthday.

Setting good and bad examples

There are examples of long-serving politicians choosing to plan their exit closer to standard retirement age.

One is Barbara Boxer. After more than three decades in Congress, the 74-year-old California Democrat announced in January 2015 that she would not seek reelection to the U.S. Senate the following year. “There is a time when you want the next generation to step in and step up,” she said.

Boxer’s early decision gave prospective successors nearly two years to organize and voters the opportunity to choose among them. Kamala Harris won the seat but stepped away to serve as President Joe Biden’s vice president.

This departure offers a striking contrast with that of Boxer’s longtime colleague, Sen. Dianne Feinstein, who remained in the Senate through a lengthy health-related absence in 2023. Feinstein, also a California Democrat, died in office that September. She was 90 years old.

She served on the influential Senate Judiciary Committee, which considers federal judicial nominations, including Supreme Court nominees. During her nearly three-month absence, the committee was deadlocked on dozens of Biden nominations after Republicans refused to let the Democrats appoint a temporary replacement for her and she refused to step down.

The tragic way Feinstein’s storied political career ended illustrated what can go wrong when lawmakers keep saying “not yet” until it’s too late.

That turned out to be the case with Biden, who reluctantly ended his presidential reelection campaign in July 2024. However, several books published since then include details about how his inner circle initially advised him to run again. 

A rushed attempt at succession followed Biden’s abrupt withdrawal from the race. Harris became the Democratic nominee without participating in any of the 2024 primaries.

When change finally came, it arrived under duress rather than by design. And Harris lost the election to Donald Trump.

Fearing what might follow

U.S. Rep. Kay Granger, a Texas Republican, announced in 2023 that she would not seek reelection the following year. It soon became clear that severe health problems were preventing her from serving her constituents.

The former House Appropriations Committee chair didn’t cast a vote in her final six months in office for a good reason: She had dementia and was staying in a Texas assisted-living facility that provided memory care services to some residents. Granger died in August 2026 at 83.

U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell, a former Senate majority and minority leader, has announced that he will step down when his current term – the Kentucky Republican’s seventh – ends in January 2027. But a fall, hospitalization and subsequent stint in a rehabilitation center in mid-2026 prompted renewed public scrutiny of the 84-year-old’s health and ability to complete his term. 

U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley of Iowa, who turned 93 on Sept. 17, 2026, and appears to be in good health, has not yet said whether he’s running for a ninth six-year term in 2028. But the Republican, who is the oldest person serving in Congress, has urged his constituents to vote for a Republican for governor.

“I don’t plan on dying in office, but if I did, I don’t want a Democratic governor choosing my successor,” Grassley said at a political event in Des Moines in late September 2026.

Learning from palliative care

My colleagues and I found an unlikely way to think differently about leadership transitions: considering lessons about letting go from palliative care.

Leaving political office or another leadership role, of course, is not the same as dying. But, as is true before someone develops a terminal medical condition, advance planning is most useful while people can still articulate what matters to them and exercise meaningful choices about what comes next.

I’ve learned that it’s a mistake to treat succession as something to discuss only when a leader must move on for health or other reasons. So, in addition to my work as a management professor, and to inform my research, as well as the workshops I hold for aging business owners and members of their inner circles, I have been trained as an end-of-life doula. I decided to do this because I lacked the vocabulary and tools that facilitated difficult conversations and decisions about their legacy and what is important to the leader as they let go.

Palliative care supports the act of letting go long before death – the same challenge confronting business leaders and the companies they run. 

When voters consider whether to vote for an aging incumbent, they may wonder whether that lawmaker is already too old for their demanding job or soon will be. But that may be the wrong question. It might be better to ask whether the legislators who represent you, no matter their age, have a plan for letting go.
news.summary: Many older incumbents are on the ballot for the 2026 midterms, adding to America’s debate over the wisdom of aging politicians delaying their retirement.
news.author: Clinical Associate Professor of Innovation and Entrepreneurship,Nancy Forster-Holt,University of Rhode Island

news.text:
On CBS's 60 Minutes on Sunday, Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito indicated that retirement is something that may be in his plans in the not too distant future, which raises several interesting scenarios, especially if the Dems take the Senate in November. On Monday's The Arena, CNN host Kasie Hunt seemed to be pushing for the Democrats to block nominees for the remainder of Trump's term if they win.

First, Hunt asked her guest Rep Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), who would be in line to become Chairman of the Judiciary Committee with a Democrat takeover of the House, who his first subpoena would go to, she played a clip of Kamala Harris, helping her push a left-wing conspiracy that Republicans might not seat victorious Democrats. Raskin responded that "in the Trump era, anything is realistic." 

Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.) proclaimed he would seek to block incoming Democrat Darializa Avila Chevalier over remarks she made about using the American flag as a napkin. But if Democrats have the majority, that's a symbolic move.

Then Hunt played a clip of Alito's interview, where they talked about retirement. "It's something I think that, um, somebody at my age has to think about every term."

Hunt then presented Raskin with the retirement scenario, and asked a bizarre question.

HUNT: So Alito is 76 years old.... If Democrats do control the Senate, would you urge your colleagues in the Senate, would you expect your colleagues in the Senate, to refuse to fill a vacancy that might be created if Alito or another Justice were to leave the court while President Trump was still President? 

Refuse to bring a nomination to the Supreme Court to a vote for a possible two-year period? Unprecedented and a bit insane. Raskin wasn't sure what she meant.

RASKIN: So if you mean, if he were actually to try and resign right after November 3rd, if the Democrats take the Senate back, so the a-- 'HUNT: What Mitch McConnell did right, where he was waiting for the election.

That is not the question Hunt asked, but she wound up settling for Raskin's interpretation of it.

RASKIN: There would be absolute outrage in the country. If you have a lame-duck president essentially barreling through in a matter of eight weeks, the nomination of a Supreme Court Justice, so a lame-duck Senate can approve and confirm that person. Remember, they held up my constituent, Merrick Garland, for 11 months when he was nominated.HUNT: So that's what I mean. And if the Democrats do take the Senate and you are in charge of the Senate and a conservative Justice steps down while Trump is still President, should Democrats do something similar and hold the vacancy open for a long period of time?

Raskin responded, now understanding what Hunt had originally asked him.

RASKIN: Oh, I see you're talking about for the next two years. Well, of course, all of that would depend on who he nominates....I mean, if he wants to appoint Donald Trump Jr. a Supreme Court Justice, I am certain that I would hope that every Democrat, every Democrat would try and stop that from happening.

But that wasn't good enough for Hunt, who seemed to be looking for a commitment from Raskin for her proposed two year ban on Trump nominees, but he wasn't biting.

HUNT: If the Democratic leaders control the floor, yes, you would be open to them confirming a Trump justice if in fact that person was suitable or you think they should refuse to seat anyone?RASKIN: They will render advice and consent according to their constitutional duty. And I fully expect the Democrats to do that....We're coming through a period of massive court packing, right wing court packing by MAGA, by Mitch McConnell, just like they kept Merrick Garland off the Court by denying him a hearing, then they barreled through the nomination of Amy Coney Barrett.

When Democrats get repeatedly grilled on TV, it's often from the left. Why aren't you are ruthless as the Republicans? 

HUNT: You're saying Democrats shouldn't use those tactics, even though Republicans have been willing to.

Of course Hunt never quoted Mitch McConnell expressing why he denied Garland a vote, after lame duck Obama nominated him in March of election year 2016. McConnell said, "The nomination should be made by the president the people elect in the election that's underway right now." He was also echoing similar feelings expressed by Senator Joe Biden in 1992, but that too was ignored by Hunt.

The trashing of McConnell and the current Court continued, and you can see that on the video below.

Pushing for an unprecedented two year moratorium on voting for SCOTUS nominees...this is CNN!

news.title: Trump Is Losing Ground With Latino Voters: Economy and Deportations Fuel The Midterm Shift.
news.text: Latino voters are moving sharply away from President Donald Trump and the Republican Party ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, reversing some of the GOP's biggest gains from 2024 as frustration over the economy and immigration enforcement grows, according to a new survey.The NBC News/Telemundo poll shows a particularly significant shift on respondents' assessment of Trump's handling of the economy, an issue that helped the president make historic inroads with Latino voters during the presidential election.Two years ago, Latino voters gave Trump a 4-point advantage over then-Vice President Kamala Harris when asked who would better handle the economy. Now, Democrats hold a 21-point advantage over Republicans on the same issue.The political consequences could be significant in November. Democrats currently lead Republicans by 24 points, 59% to 35%, when Latino voters are asked which party they want to control Congress. That advantage is twice the Democratic margin recorded at the same point in the 2024 election cycle.Nearly one in five Latinos who voted for Trump in 2024 are also no longer supporting Republican control of Congress. Fourteen percent now favor Democrats, while another 8% are undecided.Trump's overall approval rating among Latino voters has fallen to 27%. "What we can really say from this data is that 2024 was the outlier," Republican pollster Micah Roberts of Public Opinion Strategies, which surveyed Democratic firm Hart Research Associates, told NBC News.Roberts called Latinos "the swingiest of swing groups" and described the movement since the presidential election as "stunning." Economic anxiety appears to be driving much of the change. Inflation and the cost of living ranked as the top concern, cited as the most important issue by 33% of Latino voters. Nearly two-thirds, 63%, said their family income is falling behind the cost of living.Trump received particularly poor marks on those financial issues. Seventy-eight percent disapprove of his handling of the cost of living, and 74% disapprove of his handling of the economy. Another 65% believe Trump's policies have hurt economic conditions, compared with 23% who say they have helped. Among Latino independents, 72% say Trump's policies have hurt the economy.Immigration is creating another vulnerability as two-thirds of Latino voters said the Trump administration's immigration enforcement policies have gone too far. While 83% support deporting undocumented immigrants who have committed serious crimes, only 37% support deporting every undocumented immigrant in the country.The effects of the administration's enforcement campaign also appear to be reaching deeply into Latino communities. Thirty-one percent said they or someone close to them has begun carrying identification because of concerns about ICE enforcement, while 27% said they know someone who has been detained or deported by ICE during the past two years.Those numbers could particularly matter in congressional races in Florida, Texas and other states where Republicans benefited from Trump's improved performance with Latino voters in 2024. They could also affect statewide contests in Texas and Nevada.Seventy-two percent of Latino voters rated their interest in the midterms a 10 out of 10, up from 54% at the same point in 2024. Fifty-four percent said their vote this November is intended to send a message of opposition to Trump, compared with 21% who want to express support for him.Latino voters appear to be moving away from Republicans faster than they are moving toward the Democratic Party, however. Sixty-two percent now hold negative views of the GOP, up 16 points from 2024. Yet Democrats have not improved their own image as 42% view the party negatively, four points higher than two years ago.Democratic pollster Aileen Cardona-Arroyo said opposition to Trump and dissatisfaction with the economy may be enough to benefit Democrats in 2026, but the party still faces a longer-term challenge in building affirmative support.The NBC News/Telemundo poll surveyed 800 registered Latino voters from Sept. 21 through Sept. 28 by telephone and online. Twenty percent of interviews were conducted in Spanish. The survey has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points.

news.title: Trump is fueling a culture of misogynistic impunity | Robert Reich
news.text:
Last month, a young woman filed a lawsuit against Cornell University, alleging that two years ago the university had failed to protect her from being raped by seven men at a fraternity house near the university campus. She also sued the fraternity.

The lawsuit has plunged the university into a crisis and invited criticism of the district attorney, Matthew Van Houten, who decided there wasn’t enough evidence to bring criminal charges against the seven men.

At this point, we can only guess why neither Cornell nor Van Houten did more in response to the young woman’s allegations. But there’s little question that we’re living through a time when men feel some impunity when it comes to attacking women.

Violence against women is hardly new. Nor is the impunity that some men feel in attacking them.

But the man now occupying the White House has contributed to a lower and more dangerous standard for what men can do to women with impunity.

Trump was found in civil court to have sexually abused the writer E. Jean Carroll. He has repeatedly insulted the physical appearance of female journalists, politicians and public figures. He was caught on a hot microphone boasting about using his fame to forcefully kiss and grope women without consent, stating that being a star allows men to “do anything” and “grab ’em by the pussy.”

When women have spoken out against him, Trump has resorted to smear campaigns, as he did with Carroll, Stormy Daniels and Hillary Clinton. When women have stood up to him, he has exploded in anger against them, as he did with Megyn Kelly, Rosie O’Donnell, Kamala Harris, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

His administration is the most belligerently misogynistic of any in memory. It has openly equated testosterone levels to strength, conducted a cage match on the White House lawn as part of its celebration of America’s 250th anniversary, fired senior female officials, and accused the Democratic party of being run by “a bunch of childless cat ladies”.

Nor do I think it irrelevant that Trump, JD Vance and Trump’s erstwhile pal Elon Musk inhabit what’s been termed the “manosphere” – a place where the main events are dominance and submission. The whole point is to humiliate weak men and to subjugate women.

An implicit promise of the 2024 Trump campaign was to restore patriarchy to America. Fifty-four per cent of men supported Trump in that year’s election.

After Trump’s re-election, sexist and abusive attacks on women – such as “your body, my choice” and “get back in the kitchen” – surged across social media, according to an analysis from the Institute for Strategic Dialogue.

A remarkable number of Trump’s cronies are sexual harassers and predators. Trump was introduced at the Republican national convention by Dana White, chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, who was once caught on tape slapping his wife in a nightclub.

JD Vance has claimed men in America are “suppressed” in their masculinity.

Before becoming Trump’s defense secretary, Pete Hegseth paid off a woman who accused him of sexual assault. (Hegseth’s own mother accused him of abusing women, though she later disavowed her words. He has denied the claims.) And as secretary, Hegseth has championed “high-T” men and blocked promotions of female officers.

One of Elon Musk’s companies, SpaceX, reportedly paid $250,000 to a flight attendant who said Musk had exposed himself to her, though he denies the allegation. In a lawsuit filed last year, former employees accused him of “treating women as sexual objects to be evaluated on their bra size”.

After kissing Trump’s derriere, Mark Zuckerberg, the third-richest person in the US, called for more “masculine energy” because the corporate world was becoming “culturally neutered”. He told Joe Rogan: “Having a culture that celebrates the aggression a bit more has its own merits that are really positive.”

The Trump regime celebrated toxic masculinity by smoothing the way for Andrew and Tristan Tate to be extradited from Romania to the United States. The Tate brothers had been accused of luring women to Romania and then forcing them to work as pornographic webcam performers. Britain is also investigating the Tate brothers for rape and human trafficking. (US marshals arrested the Tate brothers in Miami on 18 July, following an extradition request from the United Kingdom. They’ve denied all charges.)

“I’m a Trump fan because I’m a man,” Tate has said. “You have to support Trump if you’re a man.”

Trump’s authoritarian manosphere is organized around a hierarchy topped by heroic male warriors. Winning is all about getting other males to submit to the dominant male. Women are relegated to subservient roles.

Anything that challenges the traditional heroic male roles of protector, provider and controller of the family is considered a threat to the social order. LGBTQ+ people are believed to weaken the heroic male. Hence, Trump’s executive order declaring that the US government will recognize only a person’s sex assigned at birth, limit the definition of a “male” or “female” to their reproductive cells, and potentially withhold federal funding from programs that acknowledge transgender people or “gender ideology”.

I don’t want to oversimplify a complex social phenomenon or engage in the same kind of gender stereotypes that the manosphere promotes. Male domination is hardly the only characteristic that unites Trump, Vance, Hegseth, Kennedy Jr, Musk, and the tech bros. Misogyny is not unique to authoritarian men.

Nor do I presume to know what happened at the Cornell fraternity house two years ago. But I don’t think it unreasonable to see it related to a climate of distrust bordering on hate, fostered by Trump and his administration against people who seem weak or feminine.

 Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

news.title: These are the most competitive November races up and down Texas’ midterm ballot
news.text:
With Republicans bracing for a difficult midterm election, Texas appears to have its biggest slate of competitive races for the Texas Legislature and U.S. Congress in years. The Texas Tribune has compiled a list of the most competitive general election contests, a measure of which are most likely to flip. 

We evaluated all legislative and congressional districts in Texas up for election this year, spanning 38 U.S. House seats, all 150 seats in Texas House and 16 of the 31 seats in the Texas Senate. We assigned each a rating, with the most competitive battlegrounds tagged as “hot” and the least contentious as “cold.” Some districts had less competitive heat but could still be in the mix during a wave year; we rated those as “warm.” 

For our analysis, we looked at how each district voted in the 2024 presidential and 2018 U.S. Senate elections. The closer the margins, the likelier the 2026 race would be hot. 

We also considered whether an incumbent is running for reelection and, if so, whether the incumbent outperformed their party’s presidential nominee within the district in 2024. Other factors included polling trends, such as the leftward shift of Latino voters when we weighed the “hotness” of districts in the Rio Grande Valley, and which districts the parties have identified as being on their radar. 

Enter your address below to see which candidates are running in your home districts and how we rated the competitiveness of each race. (Don’t worry: We never sell your information).

To see all of your federal, state, county and local races, use our tool to view your local ballot. 

Note: The data we used for previous elections’ margins comes from the Texas Legislative Council, which allows us to analyze the results of the 2024 and 2018 elections as if they occurred under district boundaries that are in place for this year’s elections.

All four of the state’s most competitive U.S. House races are in majority-Hispanic districts across South Texas, and each went for President Donald Trump by 10 points or more in 2024. In that election, Hispanic voters in South Texas made large shifts toward the Republican Party. 

Three of these districts are among the Democratic seats targeted by the Texas GOP’s redrawn congressional map, which was designed to net the party up to five more seats in the U.S. House.

Under the new boundaries, Trump won Districts 28, 34 and 35 each by about 10 points. But in 2018, the new 28th and 34th Districts would have been carried by Democratic Senate nominee Beto O’Rourke. Reps. Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez, the Democratic incumbents, are banking on their crossover appeal and the GOP’s sagging Latino support to overcome the mid-decade redraw.. 

In District 35, however, U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz would have beaten O’Rourke by less than half of a percentage point. Democrats also lack the advantage of incumbency here, with Rep. Greg Casar running in another district and leaving District 35 open. 

Democrats are playing offense, meanwhile, in another one of Texas’ most competitive U.S. House races. Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz is running against Tejano musician Bobby Pulido in a redrawn District 15 that now includes southeastern Hidalgo County and part of the Coastal Bend. 

Other congressional races to watch include District 9, which includes the eastern Houston area, and District 23, a sprawling and largely rural district that runs from San Antonio to the outskirts of El Paso. Neither has an incumbent running. Trump would have won both districts by at least 15 points last cycle, but the margins would have been slimmer in the 2018 U.S. Senate race. 

Texas House

At least a dozen Texas House districts are highly competitive, the majority of which Trump won by less than 10 points in 2024. About half of the most competitive races are in major urban areas or their surrounding suburbs, such as the Austin, Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston and San Antonio regions.

Republicans control an 88-62 majority in the Legislature’s lower chamber. Democrats would need to flip 14 seats to gain control of the House, though they could still change the shape of next year’s legislative session — and make governing difficult for Republicans — if they significantly narrow the GOP’s advantage.

In 2018, Democrats rode O’Rourke’s coattails to a 12-seat pickup in the Texas House.

Several of the most competitive races are also concentrated in South Texas, where Democrats see a chance to win back previously blue seats if Latino voters abandon the GOP.

In Corpus Christi’s District 34, a seat where 71% of the eligible voting population is Hispanic, Republican state Rep. Denise Villalobos outperformed the top of the ticket in 2024, winning by a margin of 9.3 points compared to Trump’s 1.4-point edge. But In the 2018 U.S. Senate election, O’Rourke won the district by 16.5 points, leaving room for Democratic challenger Stephanie Guerrero Sáenz to flip the seat.

Democrats are also targeting the Valley’s District 37, which state Rep. Janie Lopez, R-San Benito, brought under GOP control in 2022.

And in North Texas, they are going after perennial targets Morgan Meyer and Angie Chen Button, whose Dallas County districts each went for Trump by under 6 points in 2024.

Texas Senate

Only 16 of the 31 Texas Senate seats are up for election this year, an overwhelming majority of which have incumbents seeking reelection. 

The most competitive race is Senate District 9 in the northern Fort Worth area. Democratic state Sen. Taylor Rehmet took office months ago after he won a special election, flipping the GOP district that Trump previously won by 17 points.

He faces his special election opponent, Republican Leigh Wambsganss, for a rematch in November. 

The surprising upset in SD 9, paired with the buzz surrounding Democratic U.S. Senate nominee James Talarico at the top of the ticket, has energized Texas Democrats as they look to make gains statewide and flip GOP-leaning suburban districts.

Additionally, Districts 19 and 21 along the Mexico border, both controlled by Democrats, are rated as warm. Democratic 2024 presidential candidate Kamala Harris won them by slim margins, at 1 point and 3 points, respectively.
news.summary: Texas has an unusually large slate of competitive races for the state Legislature and U.S. House this year. Here’s our list of contests to watch.
