news.title: Republicans pivot to Kansas amid tight Marshall-Hamilton Senate race. ‘It’s real now’
news.text:
On the day he secured the Republican nomination in Kansas, U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall projected confidence that national Republicans could spend their precious campaign resources elsewhere.

“We’re hoping we don’t need them,” Marshall told Fox News at the time.

Now, as his reelection campaign enters its final month, the top fundraising arm for Senate Republicans is wading into Kansas in a race that could prove pivotal in determining which party controls the Senate for the last two years of President Donald Trump’s term.

Senate Leadership Fund, a national GOP-aligned political action committee, recently pivoted away from a North Carolina race and set its sights on an advertising campaign bolstering Marshall, according to multiple national news outlets.

The shift in strategy comes as Marshall is embroiled in a bitter race against the Rev. Adam Hamilton, who has billed himself as a moderate Democrat. Kansas Democrats have long struggled in Senate races, but recent polling shows the race tightening as both candidates continue to draw national attention.

The PAC’s entry into the race illustrates that national Republicans view the matchup between Marshall and Hamilton as neck and neck, said Bob Beatty, a political science professor at Washburn University who closely tracks Kansas political campaigns.

“It was real before, but it’s real now,” Beatty said of the race.

Voters’ perception of Hamilton

The national PAC on Saturday launched its first ad attacking Hamilton. The ad, which the PAC posted on social media, casts the pastor as a “two-faced extremist.” The commercial frames Hamilton as closely tied to national progressive issues.

It superimposes the pastor’s face with the faces of former Democratic presidential nominees Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris as well as Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez from New York.

Two independent polls released over the last month suggest that Kansas voters view Hamilton more favorably than Marshall. But Beatty said a high proportion of voters do not have strong feelings about Hamilton yet, a situation that allows the PAC to try to define the Democratic pastor.

“There’s still a lot of voters that don’t know anything about Adam Hamilton, and that’s what they’re going to target,” Beatty said. “That is going to be a relentless, nonstop negative ad attack.”

Before the PAC’s entry into Kansas, Hamilton’s challenge to Marshall had already drawn national attention. Across the country, Republicans are preparing for a tough battle this year amid economic concerns, the ongoing war with Iran and Trump’s poor polling numbers.

Sen. Tim Scott, a South Carolina Republican who chairs the National Republican Senatorial Committee, acknowledged in a recent interview with Semafor that the race in Kansas was close.

“It’s a very competitive state, more competitive than I’d like to see it. But the fact of the matter is that we’re going to win in Kansas,” Scott said, according to the outlet. “It’ll be closer than I want it to be.”

But Hamilton will also have to contend with the political reality of Kansas, a state that has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932. Cook Political Report, which tracks congressional races, cast the race as leaning Republican in late September.

State of the race in Kansas

A series of independent polls have portrayed the race as a dead heat.

A New York Times/Siena survey of likely Kansas voters released Saturday registered both candidates at 45% support. An Emerson College and Nexstar Media survey from the middle of September gave Hamilton a 1.5% edge over Marshall — within the poll’s 3.6% margin of error.

A spokesperson for Senate Leadership Fund did not respond to a request for comment on its reallocation of resources to Kansas and the state of the race. Marshall’s campaign declined to comment.

Tyson Brody, a spokesperson for Hamilton’s campaign, characterized the influx of GOP spending as a last-ditch effort to avoid losing a seat in a state that wasn’t supposed to be a battleground.

“Washington is panicking over desperate failing politician Roger Marshall,” Brody said in a statement that accused the incumbent of attempting to distract from his support for the war in Iran and his voting record on health care and cost-of-living issues.

As the race enters its final month, Beatty, the political science professor, said Republicans are expecting Democrats to perform well nationally.

At the same time, however, “almost everything has to go right for the Democrats” to pull off an upset win in Kansas, he said.

“On Election Day, we could be standing there that evening and Hamilton could pull off this incredible victory or Marshall wins by eight,” Beatty said.
news.author: Kacen Bayless,Matthew Kelly

news.title: SPECIAL REPORT: Apple News Blacks Out DNC’s Millions in Debt Ahead of Midterms
news.text:
Apple News, one of the most influential digital news aggregation apps, failed to promote stories about one of the Democratic National Committee’s (DNC) largest financial crises in its history despite the national implications of the matter.

The DNC’s cash-on-hand balance is currently less than its total debt, which has varied between $15 million and $18 million in recent months, primarily due to a loan secured with its headquarters as collateral. The financial woes at the DNC stand in stark contrast to its political rival, the Republican National Committee, and its sister organizations, the NRSC and NRCC, which most recently disclosed that they collectively had more than $230 million in the bank and no debt.

The DNC’s multimillion-dollar debt, much of which stems from former Vice President Kamala Harris’s failed presidential campaign in 2024 and is the largest debt it has faced since 2016, is also one of its most embarrassing financial crises, raising questions about party leadership, financial management and the fallout from the 2024 campaign.

MRC’s Findings:

Apple News failed to promote a single story about the DNC’s debt among its top 20 stories from Jan. 1 through Sept. 28, effectively shielding the Democrat shortfall from public view less than a year into President Donald Trump’s second term and months ahead of the 2026 midterms.The omission is no small matter given that party leaders have been loudly sounding alarm bells for months, resulting in widespread coverage from a wide variety of ideologically diverse news outlets during the nine months. No less than 78 stories about the DNC’s debt were published by those outlets, and none of them were promoted by Apple News.At least 14 stories about the DNC debt that Apple News could have shared were published by one of Apple News’ top 10 most promoted outlets.

Why Apple News’ Bias by Omission Matters

Apple News has effectively become one of the fastest-growing gatekeepers of information, amassing 125 million monthly views. Its influence only stands to grow as the news app comes preinstalled on virtually every modern iPhone, while its ability to drive massive audiences has proven lucrative for the news outlets it promotes.

In some cases, publishers have credited Apple News with throwing a lifeline to failing news outlets. By the media’s own accounts, stories promoted by Apple News can receive anywhere from 1 million and to as many as 20 million pageviews. 

In practice, Apple News’ massive reach and decision not to promote the DNC’s cash blunder means that millions of Americans who rely on the news aggregator for information were kept in the dark about the financial crisis plaguing Democrats.

Apple’s bias by omission is par for the course, as revealed in previous MRC analyses. For instance, MRC found that Apple News, alongside its competitor Google News, failed to promote any coverage of scandals dogging Democratic Senate candidates Graham Platner of Maine and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.

Separate MRC analyses have found that Apple News’ editors have largely excluded right-leaning outlets from its top 20 morning stories while repeatedly promoting some of the most left-leaning news outlets in the country.

The DNC Debt Crisis Coverage Apple News Left Out

The DNC, the Democratic Party’s main governing body and national organization, is the recipient of Apple News's apparent strategic editorial decision.

The financial struggles of the DNC began after Vice President Kamala Harris plowed through $1.5 billion in her failed presidential campaign in 2024. Her campaign left the DNC with an enormous debt of $20.5 million, prompting the committee to take out a $15 million loan in October 2025 to support its efforts in the off-year elections for the governors of Virginia and New Jersey. But despite the respective victories in those elections, the DNC kicked off 2026 with $17.5 million in debt, as reported by the left-wing New York Times.

The staggering debt, coming ahead of what the DNC itself billed as the “critical midterm elections,” served as a major sign of political struggle for the party, according to several news outlets. The last time the party was in this much debt was in February 2014, when it reported owing nearly $16 million.

In response, efforts to remove DNC Chair Ken Martin began, donors started directing their contributions to other leftist groups and some Democrats started to question the party's "very purpose entirely," as noted by Politico.

The DNC Debt Story Was Everywhere, Except on Apple News

Apple News’ decision not to promote the DNC budgetary shortfall is notable given the abundance of coverage available, particularly stories from a politically diverse pool of outlets that either focused on or mentioned the DNC’s debt controversy. 

MRC identified a total of 78 stories from various news outlets, including Fox News, the New York Post and the Washington Examiner, as well as Politico and others. Out of the 78 stories, 14 were from outlets that Apple News frequently promoted in its top 10. These publications included The Guardian, The New York Times (Apple News publishes Times’ sports page The Athletic), The Wall Street Journal, The Washington Post and USA Today.

The diverse sources of online stories mean that Apple News had plenty of opportunities to highlight the controversy in its daily offerings.

Among the headlines Apple News could have promoted but didn’t were:

“Debt-ridden Democrats tap a surprising asset as collateral for $15M loan,” by Fox News, published July 27.

“Inside the Phone-Throwing Drama at the Troubled, Broke Democratic Party,” by The New York Times, published July 26.

“Some Democratic donors frustrated with DNC chair Ken Martin amid fundraising woes,” by ABC News, published May 7.

“DNC cash crunch persists despite Democratic momentum heading into 2026,” by the Washington Examiner, published April 25.

“The DNC expected big money after big Democratic wins. It never came,” by The Washington Post, published April 10.

“DNC chair faces growing scrutiny amid financial pressure and internal turmoil,” by The Guardian, published July 27.

“Raging DNC boss Ken Martin threw phone at aide’s desk as committee forced to put up HQ as loan collateral: report,” by the New York Post, published July 26.\

“‘It’s beyond embarrassing’: Ken Martin and the DNC have a 2028 problem, donors warn,” by Politico, published July 31.

Apple’s omission of the Democrats’ monetary woes is particularly striking because Apple News’ top stories are manually curated by human editors, in contrast to competitors such as Google News and Microsoft’s MSN, which purportedly rely more on algorithmic selection. In other words, Apple’s editors passed over a major political story despite extensive coverage from outlets the news app routinely promotes. Why did it choose not to cover the DNC debt controversy? Only Apple can say.

MRC’s findings come on the heels of a separate analysis showing that the morning and evening shows on ABC, CBS and NBC also omitted coverage of another DNC-tied scandal: allegations that ActBlue failed to block potentially unlawful foreign donations. MRC reported on Sept. 23 that ABC News, CBS News and NBC News had aired no coverage of the ActBlue allegations from Sept. 14 through Sept. 21, a period that overlapped with the timeline examined in this study. The allegations, which could potentially trigger criminal investigations, stemmed from a 112-page report released by the House Judiciary, Oversight and Administration committees.

Methodology: The Media Research Center analyzed the top 20 stories promoted by Apple News at approximately 8:30 a.m. ET from Jan. 1, 2026 through Sept. 28, 2026 for the specific search terms “DNC,” “RNC,” “Democrat,” “Martin,” “Fundraising,” “FEC,” “Debt,” “Deficit,” and “National Committee.” Specifically, MRC sought to identify stories pertaining to the Democratic National Committee’s debt crisis and related topics. 

MRC researchers searched online for stories about the DNC’s debt from Jan. 1 through Sept. 28 that Apple News could have promoted among its top 20 stories, resulting in a tally of 78 stories. Of those, MRC identified 10 stories from outlets that Apple News routinely features among its top 20. Researchers also verified that the publishers of the identified stories were available on Apple News, addressing potential claims that the platform could not have featured them. Apple News does not feature The New York Times itself, though it does offer the newspaper’s sports section, The Athletic.

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed Is Constantly Asked About Jewish Voters. That’s Not Who He Really Has to Worry About.
news.text:
At 3 p.m. on a recent Saturday afternoon, in a conference room inside Fellowship Chapel in Detroit, Abdul El-Sayed looked different from the Senate candidate I had been watching at rallies around Michigan. He dipped his head. His voice seemed softer. This was not a room he commanded.

Almost everyone in the room besides El-Sayed was Black. He quickly tried to make inroads. “Many folks in this room are people I worked with in the city of Detroit,” he said at one point. Then, turning toward one woman he knew from those years: “Ms. Pam, have I changed at all?” he asked her. “No.” “Still talking about the same things, right?” he asked, smiling. “Yes, sir,” she said.

The women around El-Sayed belonged to the Woman Difference Collaborative, an invitation-only network of Black women faith leaders founded by the Rev. Jessica Ingram. Its members included senior pastors, first ladies, evangelists, and other women with constituencies of their own that travel far in a state like Michigan. The group began as a support system for women navigating leadership in the Black church, but its reach extended into politics. When Kamala Harris became the Democratic nominee in 2024, the collaborative organized a major gathering in support of her with only a few weeks’ notice.

Some in the room already liked El-Sayed. But most had voted for his Democratic primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens. Before El-Sayed spoke, the moderator, Monica G. Anthony, had already indicated part of the reason why: his support for the “uncommitted movement” in 2024, which many Black Democrats believed had weakened Harris on her way to losing Michigan. Some Black Democrats experienced that campaign, which demanded an end to U.S. support for Israel’s assault on Gaza, as an attack on a historic candidate they desperately wanted to elect. (Last month, in an apparent effort to help mend the wound, Harris traveled to Michigan to campaign for El-Sayed.)

Now questions still surround his campaign about whether he can win over the Black voters who largely rejected him in the primary. El-Sayed won the primary by a single percentage point. He lost in Detroit by 28 points; Stevens won the city handily.

In nearly every major national interview with El-Sayed, he’s asked about the concerns of Jewish voters in Michigan, who make up about 1.5 percent to 2 percent of voters there. He’s rarely asked about the concerns of Black voters, who make up roughly 11 percent to 12 percent. Democrats traditionally do not have a plausible path to statewide victory without a strong Black voter turnout. And if a recent Washington Post poll is any indication, El-Sayed still has a lot of ground to make up with those voters. About 83 percent of Black voters said they wanted Democrats to control the Senate—but only 67 percent said they’d back El-Sayed.

For some Black voters, the skepticism has to do with questions about El-Sayed’s progressive agenda. Others indeed cite the uncommitted movement. But the reluctance isn’t always necessarily ideological. Basil Smikle, a political strategist and professor at Columbia University, has argued that Black voters often vet candidates through a different lens than some other groups do. “The question is ultimately about familiarity, affinity, and allyship—not as symbolic gestures, but as evidence accumulated over years of shared political struggle. It is a proxy for trust,” he wrote. Stevens, many analysts noted, was a known commodity to many Black voters as a congresswoman. El-Sayed was not.

By now, many Black Democrats have made clear that they intend on voting for him. (Recently, his campaign was endorsed by the Congressional Black Caucus.) But even among them, there’s voters who say they’re doing so for the sake of coalescing against El-Sayed’s Republican opponent. Detroit attorney and former mayoral candidate Todd Perkins said he’ll probably vote for El-Sayed despite grievances about uncommitted and what he saw as patronizing outreach to Black voters. “He engages the white construct in a way that’s intelligent and everything, and then I see this commercial where he’s sitting there playing Aretha Franklin and he’s dancing a jig,” he said.

There was also a more complicated tension with the long and sometimes fraught relationship between Black and Arab communities in metro Detroit. Arab-owned gas stations, liquor stores, and other small businesses have for decades operated in predominantly Black neighborhoods, even as many of their owners lived elsewhere, producing what some Black Detroiters describe as a relationship that can feel extractive in a way that hurts their community. At a press conference in August in Detroit, an older Black man shouted, “He’s an Arab—he don’t care nothing about Black folks.” At a September roundtable with Black elected officials, Michigan state House candidate Kimberly Fisher warned that Black voters in her district brought up his race repeatedly. “Why would I vote for an Arab? Arabs don’t like us. He’s Egyptian, y’all. We don’t care. And when they see you, that’s what they see,” she said. “I’m fearful because I’m seeing more John James signs and Mike Rogers signs in the hood,” referring to El-Sayed’s Republican opponent in the Senate race.

The solution, she proposed, was El-Sayed planting his feet on the ground in those areas and speaking out against the bad practices of Arab business owners in Black communities. To El-Sayed’s credit, he has since talked openly about that fraught relationship. He told WDET in a radio interview that Arab and Muslim Michiganders can’t object to racism against themselves while tolerating it against their Black neighbors. “Standing up against racism is about principle,” he said.

In the church that afternoon, much of El-Sayed’s speech sounded familiar to me from his other campaign stops. But in this room, I noticed that he spent considerably more time on Black political history. After 9/11, one of the only Black teachers at his high school pulled him aside and told him, “You’ve got to learn your history, and not the history you’re going to learn in the classroom,” he said. The teacher took him to the library, where El-Sayed encountered writers like W.E.B. Du Bois, Alex Haley, Malcolm X, Frederick Douglass, and Fannie Lou Hamer. From there, he traced a line through the Civil Rights Movement and Black opposition to apartheid in South Africa.

Then he brought it all forward to Gaza to explain his support for uncommitted.

El-Sayed spoke about a friend who had lost 25 relatives to American-funded missiles. “Imagine watching your own tax dollars get used to annihilate your own cousins,” he said. Someone murmured, “Whoa.” He explained that he had backed uncommitted to force the Biden administration to confront what it was doing in Gaza. “A Democratic Party that says that it’s for human rights has got to be for human rights,” he explained. He noted that when Joe Biden quit the race, El-Sayed endorsed Harris the next day.

I looked around the room and saw that the group did seem moved. The skepticism I had heard at the beginning of the afternoon had evaporated. By the end, nine of the women gathered behind El-Sayed’s chair, and each placed a hand on him as they bowed their heads in prayer. “We thank you for the people that you put on the Earth to make change,” one of them said. “We recognize that all of us are called to something.”

He may have won the room, but El-Sayed still has to move a much larger electorate. The campaign appears to understand that this cannot be solved by simply assuming voters who usually back Democrats will eventually fall in line. Fellowship Chapel was one stop in a broader effort: The campaign says El-Sayed has visited more than two dozen Black churches and participated in more than 100 meetings and events with Black elected officials, clergy, community leaders, and organizations across the state. On Monday, former President Barack Obama announced he would travel to Detroit to stump for El-Sayed, a hard-won coup for the candidate.

The afternoon I was there, El-Sayed had another campaign stop to get to, and soon his staff was moving him toward the door. I stayed behind. The room loosened into little clusters of women catching up and talking about what came next. I wanted to know whether the prayer and applause would translate into anything.

Monica G. Anthony, the first lady of Fellowship Chapel and the wife of the Rev. Wendell Anthony, the longtime president of the Detroit NAACP, told me she had voted for Stevens in the primary and had entered the afternoon with questions about El-Sayed’s support for uncommitted. The point of bringing him into the room, she said, had been to make a judgment for themselves. “We reach a lot of people, and we need to see if you are that person,” Anthony said. “And then if you are the person, how do we make it happen to get elected?” By the end, she had made up her mind: “I think he is that person.”

Nearby, LaToya Henry, another woman with deep ties to Black civic life in Detroit, said she had not voted for El-Sayed in the primary either and came because she wanted to hear him explain himself. “I didn’t just want my vote to be like, ‘Oh, I’m picking the lesser of two evils,’ ” she told me. After hearing him walk through the decision, she said, “Now my vote is definitely not a lesser of two evils.” Her parents had also not voted for El-Sayed. They were already having similar conversations with friends, and Henry now felt equipped to take what she had heard in the room back to them.

The Rev. Patricia Coleman-Burns, a University of Michigan professor emerita who grew up in Detroit and has watched the region’s racial and political coalitions shift for more than 70 years, was a die-hard Stevens supporter. But she told me, after the primary, she began watching the political energy gathering around the man who had beaten her candidate. Hundreds turned out in Farmington Hills. Students lined up in Ann Arbor. Black clergy in Detroit came out for him. She saw similar enthusiasm in Grand Rapids, Muskegon, Battle Creek, Flint, and Saginaw. “I have seen people come alive,” she said. She had also begun feeding advice through people in El-Sayed’s orbit about how he talked to Black voters. Early in the campaign, she said, El-Sayed tended to speak broadly about people of color. Now he explicitly talked about Black people and Black communities. “He has evolved. Prior to the primary, it was a campaign,” she said. “Now it’s a movement, and it’s a movement because it’s beyond him.”
news.summary: Inside one room on a recent Saturday afternoon, I saw the problem at work.

news.title: LIZ PEEK: A blue wave? The liberal media wants one, but voters might disagree
news.text: Four weeks from today, Americans will go to the polls and set the country’s course for the next two years. Heads up to Republicans: things are shifting. The liberal media is positively giddy over polls showing Republicans lagging in key Senate races, and others showing the GOP likely to lose the House. But are their happy forecasts of a blue wave likely to prove right? Maybe, but there are signs that voters are beginning to look at Democrat candidates more closely, and they don’t like what they see. When long-time Democrat Debra Messing endorses Republican Bruce Blakeman for governor in New York State over incumbent Kathy Hochul, something is afoot. Incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins, considered vulnerable by Democrats, now leads her opponent and Michigan Democrat candidate Abdul El-Sayed just lost the endorsement of an important union. Meanwhile, in Minnesota, which went for Kamala Harris in 2024, candidate Michele Tafoya could become the first Republican senator from the state since 2009. For all they celebrate Donald Trump’s low approval ratings, the reality is that the Real Clear Polling averages put Democrats’ favorability at 39%, exactly tied with the president. The media are also playing up worst-case scenarios in a determined effort to drive down Republican turnout and campaign funds. It’s a clever strategy. If voters think their cause is lost, they may well stay home and decline to back local candidates. LEE CARTER: POLLS SAY DEMOCRATS COULD SWAMP REPUBLICANS. AS A POLLSTER, I HAVE A QUESTION Note to voters: it’s far too early to reach that conclusion. Much can change between now and November. The polls are seemingly becoming less reliable with every election cycle and can also be easily manipulated. In a recent New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena survey of Maine that shows Collins in the lead, for instance, the surprised author writes it has "a sample that looks reasonably favorable to Democrats." Even the Washington Post admits in a recent piece, "There are reasons to suspect polls could be overestimating Democrats’ strength." Meanwhile, there are signs that increased scrutiny may not bode well for the radical leftists running for senate seats in Michigan, in Maine, or elsewhere. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed recently lost the endorsement of the state’s firefighters union. The head of that labor group claims it had always meant to remain neutral in the race, which also features Republican Mike Rogers, and that El-Sayed’s name on a list of endorsements was a clerical mistake. That account is disputed by at least one union official who says it was El-Sayed’s negative views of law enforcement that soured his organization. He told a local news outfit, "Abdul El-Sayed has …held positions within organizations that support defunding the police and abolishing a considerable portion of our prison system." Republicans, digging into El-Sayed’s past, are highlighting a tweet from the candidate saying, "The fact that cops kill Black folks so regularly tells us who society considers part of the ’public’ & from whom they are to be kept safe. Its not just a few bad cops — it’s an entire SYSTEM of white supremacy." MORNING GLORY: EL-SAYED MIGHT HAVE A PROBLEM WITH THE BLACK VOTE IN MICHIGAN El-Sayed likely hoped to keep those offensive past remarks hidden, but the days of erasing history are long gone. El-Sayed is also tagged with campaigning with Hasan Piker, the infamous anti-Israel influencer who claimed America "deserved 9/11." That cannot sit well with most voters. The Michigan race is a toss-up; Real Clear Polling shows recent surveys have El-Sayed one or two points ahead of Rogers, within the margin of error. In Maine, which went for Kamala Harris by 7 points in 2024, Democratic former state Senator Troy Jackson is struggling in his bid to unseat long-serving Republican Collins. Democrats considered this race a prime pick-up opportunity — the only state won by Harris that had a GOP senator running for reelection. news.title: Mike Rogers Faces Tougher Senate Battle in Michigan Than His 2024 Near-Miss
news.text: Republican U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers of Michigan came within less than 20,000 votes of flipping a Senate seat two years ago. But in his second consecutive bid for the upper chamber, his odds of finally winning it look worse than ever. The former congressman faces a competitive race against progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who surprised many by winning the Democratic nomination and has since consistently led Rogers in public polling. FiftyPlusOne puts the race at 47.9 percent for El-Sayed and 44.3 percent for Rogers, while the 270toWin average shows a slightly wider 4-point gap, 48.4 percent to 44.4 percent. The numbers point to a tougher climb for Rogers, who chaired the House Intelligence Committee before leaving Congress in 2015. The race for the seat being vacated by retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters has been widely viewed as a key contest for both parties as they vie for control of the Senate. A Wider Gap Than 2024 Rogers' 2024 race against Elissa Slotkin, now Michigan's junior senator and a Democrat, was among the closest Senate contests in the country. Slotkin won by less than half a percentage point, even as President Donald Trump carried the state at the top of the ticket. That result established Rogers as a credible candidate in a state where Republicans have struggled to win Senate races. Party leaders recruited him to run again, betting his name recognition and narrow loss would give him a head start in an open-seat race. The early numbers have not delivered that head start. Most September polls showed Rogers trailing El-Sayed, though individual surveys varied widely. At one end, El-Sayed led by 7 points. At the other, Rogers held a small advantage. The spread reflects a race that pollsters are still struggling to pin down. It also reflects a national environment that has shifted since 2024. Rogers ran two years ago alongside a Republican presidential nominee who won Michigan. This year, he is running in a midterm with a Republican in the White House in a setting that has historically favored the party out of power. Jim Kessler of the center-left think tank Third Way told Newsweek that Democrats are heading into what is "shaping up to be a blue wave" in November. He cautioned, however, that a favorable climate does not settle a race in a state as closely divided as Michigan. "El-Sayed still has work to do to win the decisive middle in a swing state like Michigan," Kessler said. The Primary Warning While polling has been underwhelming for Republicans this cycle, with many candidates carrying the weight of a deeply unpopular administration, El-Sayed's primary result also gives Republicans a reason to see an opening in numbers that otherwise favor Democrats. Several late primary polls showed El-Sayed approaching or topping 50 percent and leading Michigan Representative Haley Stevens by double digits. While he won the nomination over the moderate Democrat, his final margin fell short of what those surveys had projected. El-Sayed won by about 1 percentage point, 48.5 percent to 47.5 percent, a margin of roughly 14,900 votes. The gap between the polls and the result does not translate neatly into the general election. Primary electorates are smaller and less predictable than November turnout, and pollsters have a harder time modeling who will actually show up. A miss in August can come from turnout assumptions that have little bearing on a statewide general election. Still, the pattern carries weight for a candidate whose lead rests on a few points. If general-election surveys are overstating El-Sayed's support by a margin similar to the primary miss, Rogers would be running roughly even rather than several points back. Michigan also has its own history with polling errors. Surveys in recent statewide cycles have at times underestimated Republican support, a concern that hangs over any modest Democratic lead in the state. "The primary is one set of voters and the general is another," Kessler said. El-Sayed built his primary campaign around progressive positions, including support for Medicare for All, and drew backing from the party's left wing. Those positions energized Democratic primary voters, but the general election will test whether he can also appeal to moderates. Former President Barack Obama and ex-Vice President Kamala Harris have both publicly endorsed his campaign. Republicans have tried to make that case directly, casting El-Sayed as too far left for a state that voted for Trump twice by highlighting his association with left-wing streamer Hasan Piker. Democrats, for their part, are expected to tie Rogers to the Trump administration and national Republican positions that poll poorly in the state. Marist's September 24 to 27 survey of 1,235 registered voters found 41 percent of Michigan voters approve of the job Trump is doing. The same poll found 42 percent say their congressional vote is mainly a vote against Trump. Republicans' Long Michigan Drought Michigan has been competitive at the presidential level for most of the last decade, but Senate races have gone a different way. Republicans have not won a Senate seat in the state since 1994. Rogers' 2024 campaign came closer than any Republican effort in years. His narrow loss showed he could hold together the coalition Trump built in the state while staying competitive in the suburbs around Detroit and Grand Rapids. Reassembling that coalition without Trump on the ballot is a separate challenge. Midterm turnout tends to be lower and more dependent on enthusiasm, and the party holding the White House often struggles to motivate its own voters. Many of the lower-propensity voters who turned out for Trump in 2024 may not return in a midterm year. The current numbers suggest Rogers is starting several points behind rather than close to even. That is a weaker position on paper than the one that produced his near-miss. The race nonetheless remains within reach for Republicans. A 3- or 4-point lead in a state with a recent record of polling misses gives El-Sayed an advantage, but a thin one. A modest, consistent error in the Democratic direction, of the kind seen in his own primary, would erase most of it. Fundraising gives El-Sayed a modest edge in total receipts, though the picture is more mixed when it comes to money available to spend. El-Sayed has raised about $14.5 million over the course of the campaign, compared with roughly $10.9 million for Rogers. Rogers, however, held more cash in mid-July filings. He reported approximately $4.47 million on hand, while El-Sayed had about $2.55 million after spending heavily in a crowded and expensive Democratic primary. With four weeks left before Election Day, both campaigns and their allies are treating Michigan as one of the few states that could determine which party controls the Senate next year. The polls will show whether El-Sayed's lead holds as the race moves into its final stretch, or whether the warning from August winds up applying in November as well. news.title: The Rise & Rise of Dan Rather
news.text:
Today, as his 95th birthday birthday approaches on Oct. 31, Rather remains engaged with news as a social media commentator, with plenty to say about the Trump administration and the state of journalism.

Rather began as a regional reporter in Texas and became chief of the network’s Southern bureau in 1963. In the first of many high-profile career moments, he organized the network’s local coverage of President John F. Kennedy’s Nov. 22, 1963, visit to Dallas, where Kennedy was assassinated.

After covering the Nixon White House, the Vietnam War and other domestic and international stories, Rather became one of television’s “Big Three” nightly news anchors in 1981. For the next two decades, Rather on CBS, Peter Jennings on ABC and Tom Brokaw on NBC, were prominent faces of the last era in which legacy media companies truly set the news agenda.

In his reporting tenure, Dan Rather repeatedly tangled with U.S. presidents. He brought that reporter’s attitude to the anchor role. Rather didn’t just preside over news stories – he was immersed in their preparation and aware of their potential impact.

I teach communication and have written about the history of television and the intersection of media and politics. In my view, the most-cited moments in Rather’s long career reflect the on-edge, on-the-scene, news-gathering spirit of legendary CBS newsman Edward R. Murrow, rather than the avuncular style of a corporate American media host.

Confronting the powerful

Murrow first became known for reporting directly from the London Blitz bombings via radio in 1940 and 1941. At home through the 1950s and 1960s, Murrow delivered unflinching TV documentary reports on subjects that included Sen. Joseph McCarthy’s pursuit of alleged communists in the federal government and harsh working conditions faced by migrant farmworkers.

As a reporter, Rather also covered stories with major national impact. Following the Kennedy assassination, he solidified his credentials as CBS’s White House correspondent during the Johnson and Nixon administrations and, in 1966, he was sent at his request to report from Vietnam.

Back stateside, Rather covered the divisive and bitter 1968 presidential campaign. As a determined floor correspondent at the Democratic National Convention in Chicago, he was knocked down on camera by security guards while trying to interview a Georgia delegate whom the guards were removing from the convention floor.

Over time, Rather was cast as Nixon’s most prominent onscreen adversary. When Nixon resigned in August 1974, Rather acquired a lasting reputation for helping to hold a U.S. president accountable.

Finding stories everywhere

After Nixon’s resignation, Rather’s presence at CBS News grew. He served as weekend news anchor and chief correspondent for the documentary series “CBS Reports,” and he joined the weekly news magazine “60 Minutes” in 1975.

One of his most-discussed reports was a 1980 story on the Russian occupation of Afghanistan. To cover the war firsthand, Rather and his team dressed in local garb and crossed the border from Pakistan into Afghanistan, where they interviewed resistance fighters and visited battle sites.

Critics praised the segment for showing U.S. audiences the stakes in a faraway conflict; they also rebuked Rather and “60 Minutes” for showboating. Washington Post media critic Tom Shales wrote, “It’s hard to decide whether Murrow is smiling down approvingly or spinning in his grave.”

In 1981, Rather won the competition to succeed Walter Cronkite as “CBS Evening News” anchor, a position he would hold for 24 years.

Rather’s style and demeanor were noticeably different from Cronkite’s reassuring cadence. Even behind the anchor desk, Rather’s inquisitive manner and reporter’s instincts for confrontation were well known. Those traits could be seen as either powerful assets or indicators of biased coverage.

Rather also continued to report, through CBS vehicles such as “48 Hours,” a show that investigated crime and justice stories, and the spinoff show “60 Minutes II.” His pursuit of international and domestic stories earned numerous Emmy and Peabody awards – more than a dozen in the 1980s alone – and he also received special honors, including his 2004 induction into the Television Academy Hall of Fame.

Exit from CBS

Rather’s trajectory changed abruptly after he reported a 2004 “60 Minutes II” segment about then-President George W. Bush’s service in the Texas Air National Guard in 1968-1974. The segment raised questions about whether Bush – whose father was former president George H.W. Bush – had received preferential treatment that kept him from being sent to fight in the Vietnam War.

Critics challenged the authenticity of some documents that CBS cited in the report, and an external review panel concluded that the network had failed to authenticate them properly. The network apologized; Rather defended the report initially but conceded after several weeks that the materials should not have been used. The debacle became known as “Rathergate.”

Rather’s CBS contract was not renewed. He left the anchor chair in 2005 and the network in 2006, asserting in his departing press statement, “I will do the work I love elsewhere.”

Before leaving CBS, Rather urged citizens and journalists alike to take on the tough battles. “Whether it’s City Hall, the Statehouse or the White House, part of our job is to speak truth to power,” Rather said in a 2006 speech in Seattle.

New platforms

Cable news offered Rather an alternative. Over the next 15 years he hosted several in-depth reporting and interview programs on cable channels. There, he embraced being a news reporter who could call his own shots and criticize people in positions of power in politics and business.

In his 80s, Rather took to social media, attracting hundreds of thousands of followers via Facebook, the social platform X, formerly Twitter, and Steady, a newsletter distributed via the Substack platform. He quickly adopted the language of short-burst online communication, using snark and style in the service of delivering solid journalism.

Speaking truth to the press

Today, the Trump administration is widely viewed as waging war on the mainstream media. President Donald Trump regularly calls journalists the “enemy of the people,” has tightly limited reporters’ access at the White House and the Pentagon, and has sued numerous media outlets for what he calls unfair or defamatory coverage.

In response, many large media companies are taking steps that critics see as pulling punches or currying favor with the Trump White House. For example, in the fall of 2025 CBS News adopted new rules that bar editing recorded interviews before they air.

This step came after the network’s parent company paid Trump US$16 million to settle a lawsuit over its editing of a 2024 interview with Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris. CBS also hired Kenneth Weinstein, a prominent conservative and former think tank executive, for a new ombudsman position.

In a Substack post, Rather called the changes evidence that CBS “has tipped over the precipice: that corporate overlords in concert with an autocratic president are demolishing support for independent journalism in favor of financial gain, and in so doing undermining a key foundation of our democracy.” His warning echoed Murrow’s famous 1958 speech urging broadcast leaders to use the power of the medium to teach, illuminate and inspire, rather than letting it become “nothing but wires and lights in a box.”

Dan Rather has pursued that mission throughout his career, even as the players and technologies have changed. He has consistently embraced the challenges, and satisfaction, of being a journalist intent on holding powerful people accountable – including the heads of news organisations.

Harry Castleman, co-author with Walter Podrazik of “Watching TV: American Television, Season by Season,” contributed to this article.

Walter Podrazik is Adjunct Lecturer in Communication, University of Illinois Chicago. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Dan Rather has followed the news wherever he goes, in a career that highlights 75 years of evolving journalism, writes Walter Podrazik

news.title: Democrats May Flip Longest-Held GOP Senate Seat for First Time in 107 Years
news.text: Democrats have their eyes on a potential upset in Kansas, where recent polls show the U.S. Senate race in a dead heat and the Cook Political Report rates the contest Lean Republican with roughly four weeks until Election Day. The position is held by Republican incumbent Senator Roger Marshall, a doctor, who is battling Democrat Adam Hamilton for the seat that has been held by the GOP since 1919, the longest ever for any party, High Plains Public Radio says. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. Republicans now hold a narrow majority in both the House and Senate. President Donald Trump carried Kansas by double digits over then-Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election, underscoring the state’s Republican tilt. But Democrats have maintained a foothold in the state, with Laura Kelly in the governor’s mansion even as Republicans hold both U.S. Senate seats. Newsweek reached out to both Marshall and Hamilton's campaigns via email on Monday for comment. What To Know According to recent polling, Hamilton either leads by a very slim margin or the race is statistically tied. However, on prediction market site Kalshi Monday night, Marshall has 66 percent versus Hamilton's 34 percent. According to prediction market site Polymarket, Marshall has 68 percent compared to 33 percent for Hamilton. Cook says Hamilton is running an "increasingly strong race" and has been launching an attack ad against Marshall, an OB-GYN, over billing and collection practices at his office. Marshall has branded the ad targeting his practice a "lie." The forecaster also highlights that agriculture—and economic concerns impacting fertilizer and gas—are major factors in the Sunflower State and the rising prices make the race more competitive. Meanwhile, Marshall has branded Hamilton as a "radical Democrat," adding that "his sermons are identical to the Democratic Party platform." Democrats are hoping to capitalize on Trump's dropping approval ratings in state and national polls as the midterm elections loom. The president's overall approval and ranking on key policy issues like the economy, immigration, jobs and the ongoing war in Iran have slipped as households across America are flagging affordability concerns. Robert Y. Shapiro, professor of political science at the School of International and Public Affairs at Columbia, told Newsweek on Monday when asked if Democrats realistically could flip the seat: "If this is a 'Wave' election it can flip. Or even otherwise since Hamilton is a very good moderate Democrat running against a very vulnerable opponent. This would be then a one off election unless this establishes a viable precedent for future Democratic candidates in Kansas. And possibly for Democrats elsewhere." What the Polls Show In a poll by The New York Times and Siena University last month, Marshall had 47 percent of the potential vote compared to 46 percent for Hamilton, and 7 percent of respondents said they did not know. The poll surveyed 605 likely voters from September 22 to September 30 and had a margin of error of 4.6 points. A Trafalgar Group poll shows Hamilton has 44.4 percent of the potential vote compared to 43.5 percent for Marshall, 2 percent for Libertarian Party candidate David C Graham and 10.1 percent are undecided. The poll surveyed 1,095 likely voters across the state from September 29 to October 1 and has a margin of error of 2.9 percent. A Wedgewood Polls survey last month showed Hamilton with 50 percent compared to Marshall's 48 percent and Graham's 2 percent. The poll surveyed 500 likely voters from September 22 to September 24 and had a 4.4 percent margin of error. Breakdown of Hamilton vs. Marshall Hamilton is pastor of the largest United Methodist Church in the country, the Church of the Resurrection. He founded the Kansas City-area church in 1990 at age 25, according to his campaign website. He won the Democratic Senate primary in August and is running on affordability; a theme Democrats across the country are emphasizing. His campaign is focused on bringing down energy, housing and healthcare costs as well as protecting Social Security, agriculture and ending “chaos and corruption” in Washington, D.C., his website says. Meanwhile, Marshall has been in the U.S. Senate since winning his 2020 election. He has been an OB-GYN in the state for 25 years, his campaign website highlights, and calls himself a fifth-generation "farm kid." Trump endorsed Marshall, labeling him a "strong advocate" for the people of Kansas. His campaign website touts bills from agriculture, border security and rural healthcare as a guide for voters to see what policies are important to the Republican. news.title: Lady with lamp and darkness
news.text:
Is a feminist allowed to pick and prioritise her agendas? Or is it that there is never a question of picking or prioritising in the first place as everything intersects and correlates in the quest for emancipatory politics of which feminist movements are important actors? These two questions contextualise the grey discussions that can emerge when we hold public figures accountable and responsible for their ideologies and politics.

Gloria Steinem, who passed away at 92, represented a fight that made American society face some tough questions concerning its exploitation of women, their bodily autonomy, the economic disparity between men and women, and the consumerist culture that commodified women. There has been some scrutiny of Steinem’s legacy after her passing on social media. Some users were seen commenting on how she “kept feminism from discussing class” as well as from the structural issues beyond liberal reforms and representation. Steinem criticised capitalist exploitation and the devaluation of women’s labour, but her politics sought feminist transformation within and across economic systems rather than treating the abolition of capitalism as the sole route to women’s liberation. This is where the scrutiny comes into play regarding her ideological positions and not-so-discreet affiliations. In internet video archives, we find interview clips of Steinem referring to the Central Intelligence Agency as a “liberal, non-violent and honorable” organisation. In 1975, a feminist collective called the Redstockings published a report establishing her affiliation with the organisation besides her directorship of the Independent Research Services that was indirectly funded by the CIA. Interestingly, in 1975, she was among 60 prominent women who condemned the UN General Assembly’s Resolution 3379, which equated Zionism with racism. Yet, Steinem’s feminism stood tall on other questions, such as those pertaining to women’s economic rights and feminist criticism of the United States of America for going to war against Vietnam and Iraq.

Her public life was not shorn of apologias. Her initial views on transsexualism argued that surgical transitions conformed to stereotyping gender roles: she later digressed from this position. Again, in 2016, she patronisingly commented that young women supported Bernie Sanders partly to meet young men: she later apologised publicly for this statement.

Following her demise, the former US secretary of state, Hillary Clinton, paid her tribute to Steinem by stating that “her activism was rooted in optimism”; the former vice-president, Kamala Harris, hailed her as a “trailblazing activist, organizer, and journalist — an icon in so many ways”. In fact, Steinem fit just too well in the mould created for an internationally-palatable, secure and commensurate feminism. She was a strong voice against the suffering of women due to war: yet she did not condemn conflict that was the consequence of Western imperialism and its nexus with global capitalist forces. Would Steinem have extended her support and solidarity to the collective resistance of women and their agencies against neocolonialism and neoliberal imperialism going beyond the language of human rights violations? Would she have condemned the decades-long American sanctions against Iran and Cuba that adversely affected Iranian and Cuban women’s health and domestic labour and led to their economic plight? Decolonial feminists have for long raised questions about the manipulation of the discourse on women’s rights and liberation as a Trojan horse, aimed at invasive intentions against the sovereignty of nation-states in the third world. Steinem’s silence on these crucial questions was noticeable in this context.

It’s difficult to not celebrate Gloria Steinem. But in a world where capitalism has succeeded in creating fragmented versions of feminisms, somehow, we end up celebrating only palatable versions of feminists. Steinem’s passing must be grieved and her legacy celebrated posthumously — for fighting the feminist battles in her own right. But feminists from other parts of the world, especially developing nations and third world countries, must continue to unapologetically examine and dissect her work and beliefs. The question is not about discrediting a feminist’s work and life; it may also not be about whom she chose not to represent or whom she chose not to raise her voice for — it’s largely about whom she overrepresented.

Radhika Jagtap teaches at the School of Law, UPES, Dehradun

news.title: Is El-Sayed Panicking About His Campaign? It Sure Looks Like It.
news.text:
Democrats in states like Minnesota and Michigan nominated Senate candidates who are not mainstream at all, and in doing so made those races ripe for the GOP to flip. Michigan is the best example. Abdul El-Sayed beat Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) in the August primary, and that made the seat far more competitive. Yes, the prediction markets still favor him over Republican Mike Rogers, but watch what El-Sayed is doing and you'll see several signs that he knows his campaign is in trouble.

I previously reported that El-Sayed flip-flopped on Medicare for All, his signature issue, mere weeks before Election Day. Candidates who are comfortably ahead don't torch their own brand in October. A campaign does that when its own numbers say it's behind.

And it really was his brand. El-Sayed spent years pushing a plan that would outlaw private insurance and herd every American onto a single government plan. He even floated repealing the Second Amendment and swapping in a constitutional right to health care. That's who Michigan Democrats picked to win over a swing state.

Related: El-Sayed’s Sister-in-Law Was on the Terror Watchlist in 2016

Now he says the opposite. "If you would like to have a private insurer, above that, you're welcome to do that," El-Sayed said. Sound familiar? It should, because former President Barack Obama sold Obamacare by promising Americans they could keep their plans, and we all remember how that turned out.

Speaking of Obama, here’s the other sign El-Sayed knows his campaign is in trouble: He is bringing him in to campaign late in the race, which suggests his internal polling isn't looking good.

More from the Associated Press:

Obama will appear with El-Sayed at an Oct. 24 rally that will also feature other top Democratic candidates in Michigan, including Jocelyn Benson, the party’s nominee for governor. Obama is getting significantly more involved in the midterm elections, with additional campaign stops and advertisements expected to come in the closing weeks, according to plans shared first with The Associated Press.The Detroit event is a notable show of support for El-Sayed, who defeated moderate Rep. Haley Stevens in an August primary and has since worked to consolidate Democratic support in his race against Republican Mike Rogers. The open seat is expected to be among a handful that will decide which party controls the majority next year.

So El-Sayed has "worked to consolidate Democratic support" since August, and less than two weeks before Election Day, he still needs a former president to fly into Detroit and finish the job for him? That’s rough. In Detroit, of all places. A Democrat who has to shore up his own party's base in its biggest stronghold that late in the race has a serious problem, no matter what the prediction markets say.

El-Sayed clearly realizes he needs help. Whether Obama can deliver it is another matter entirely. Let’s not forget that Obama campaigned for Kamala Harris in 2024 in Pennsylvania, Nevada, Wisconsin, Georgia, and even Michigan, and she lost all of those states.

So, good luck with that, Abdulrahman.

news.title: GOP's Sununu Surges in Bid to Flip Democrat's New Hampshire Senate Seat
news.text: Democrat Chris Pappas' lead appears to be diminishing versus Republican John E. Sununu in the battle for U.S. Senate in New Hampshire, as midterm elections are roughly four weeks away. A new poll released by Rasmussen Reports shows that 49 percent would vote for Pappas versus 44 percent who would pick Sununu. The five-point lead is a notable difference from a poll last month that showed Pappas with an 11-point lead over Sununu, 45 percent to 34 percent. Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen is set to retire in the Granite State, opening the seat for November's general election. The Cook Political Report rates the race as a toss-up. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. Republicans hold a narrow majority in both the House and Senate. Former Vice President Kamala Harris won New Hampshire during the 2024 presidential election over President Donald Trump by less than 3 percent. The state has not elected a Republican senator in more than 15 years. Newsweek reached out to both Sununu and Pappas' campaigns via email on Monday for comment. What To Know About the New Poll According to the new poll showing Sununu's gains, 3 percent would pick Constitution Party candidate Edmond Laplante and 4 percent are not sure. Pappas has 89 percent of Democrats' vote, 15 percent of Republicans and 40 percent of non-affiliated voters, the poll shows. Sununu has 84 percent of Republican support, 8 percent of Democrats' and 44 percent of unaffiliated voters. Pappas has a large lead with women, as 53 percent favor him versus 33 percent for Sununu, while 53 percent of men favor the Republican candidate compared to 42 percent for Pappas. The survey shows a sizable advantage for Pappas, 46, among those 65 and older, with 58 percent compared to 39 percent as Sununu, 62, who represented the Granite State in the Senate from 2003 to 2009, is favored by those under 40 years old. The poll was conducted from October 2 to October 4 among 979 likely New Hampshire voters and has a margin of error of 3 percent. News-rating website AllSides rates Rasmussen Reports as "Lean Right," adding in part that sources with that designation "moderately align with conservative, traditional, libertarian, or right-wing thought and/or policy agendas." Craig Agranoff, political professor at Florida Atlantic University, told Newsweek on Monday, "Republicans have an avenue in NH, but it is a narrow one. Sununu cutting a double digit Rasmussen lead down to 5 points fits a race Cook already calls a toss up. The Sununu name, ticket splitting, and outside money give the GOP a real shot in a state that often votes one way for governor and another for Senate. A 5 point deficit with a month left is not a win. It is a live race." Agranoff added, "Holding the Senate is not a NH only story. Republicans need this seat or a similar pickup to offset losses elsewhere. If Sununu keeps closing, it becomes part of the majority math. If the lead holds near five, it is a warning, not a path." What Other Polls Show A recent survey from the University of New Hampshire shows 50 percent would pick Pappas, 42 percent would pick Sununu, 2 percent would pick Laplante, 2 percent would write in another candidate and 4 percent are undecided. The poll was conducted from September 17 to September 21 among 1,418 likely general election voters, with a margin of error of 2.6 percent. In an August survey from the pollster, Sununu was up 45 percent compared to 43 percent for Pappas, 5 percent would have voted for another candidate and 7 percent were undecided. That poll was conducted from August 20 to August 24 among 1,878 likely general election voters, with a margin of error of 2.3 percent. The results for this survey were within the margin of error, making it a statistical tie. A co/efficient poll last month had the race deadlocked between the two at 46 percent, while 9 percent were undecided. Pappas' favorability was 37 percent compared to a 51 percent unfavorable rating and 13 percent had no opinion. Sununu's favorability was 41 percent compared to a 47 percent unfavorable rating and 12 percent had no opinion. The poll was conducted from September 9 to September 11 among 958 likely general election voters in the Granite State and had a margin of error of 3.15 percent. news.title: Obama plans Detroit rally with El-Sayed in tight Senate race
news.text:
Several polls showed Abdul El-Sayed in a close race with former Republican representative Mike Rogers, in one of the midterm's most expensive contests. (EPA Images pic)
MICHIGAN: Former president Barack Obama and president Donald Trump both plan to campaign in Michigan during the coming weeks in a showdown to bolster their candidates, especially in the key Senate race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and opponent Mike Rogers, just ahead of the Nov 3 election.
Obama’s Oct 24 appearance - coming about a month after former vice president Kamala Harris campaigned with El-Sayed - underscores the stakes for Democrats in Michigan, long seen as a must-win for the party if it wants to retake the Senate. 
In addition to El-Sayed, the rally will feature Michigan secretary of state Jocelyn Benson, who is running for governor, according to a statement Monday from the state’s Democratic Party.
Several polls show El-Sayed within the margin of error in his race against former Republican representative Mike Rogers, with the campaign becoming one of the most expensive in this midterm cycle. 
More than US$280 million has been spent on advertising so far, according to AdImpact. 
Democrats need to flip four seats to take a majority in the Senate and while more races nationally have become competitive, holding Michigan following the retirement of Democratic Senator Gary Peters is seen as essential to that effort.
Trump said at the White House on Monday that he will be in Michigan “in about a week and a half.” He was last in the state in July when he held a rally at the General Motors vehicle testing ground in Milford outside Detroit. The president has spent his time campaigning recently in the Republican-led states of Alabama and Oklahoma.
The question for Republicans is whether Trump will help Rogers. The Epic MRA poll said 57% of Michigan voters polled see Trump unfavourably. Governor Gretchen Whitmer fares next worst with a 42% unfavourable rating.
El-Sayed has been working to court Michigan’s Black voters, who largely backed his Democratic opponent during the primary. A recent poll conducted in the state by Epic MRA in late August had El-Sayed leading Rogers among all voters by 47% to 43%. The same poll had 77% of Black voters backing the Democrat.
Obama has kept a relatively low profile in midterm races so far, though he did travel to Texas to support Senate candidate James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic candidate for governor, at a taco restaurant in Austin in May.
news.summary: Barack Obama’s appearance underscores the stakes for Democrats in Michigan, a must-win state if the party wants to retake the Senate.

news.title: All Eyes on the Trump Family: Biden's FBI Tracked Melania and Barron's Movements — As Bombshell Emails Show Steps Taken in Secret Probe
news.text:
The FBI under Joe Biden’s administration allegedly monitored Melania and Barron Trump’s travel movements and tapped into future White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles’ cellphone data to help pinpoint the timing of its Mar-a-Lago search for classified and national security documents that Donald Trump was suspected of improperly keeping, RadarOnline.com can reveal. 

The armed feds executed their search on August 8, 2022, at the Palm Beach, Florida, mansion, and the Trump administration has now released a trove of documents related to Operation Plasmic Echo, which revealed bombshell information about the surveillance of Melania and Barron.'Donald Trump’s Legal Defense Team, Journalists And Campaign Advisers' Were Monitored"Already in the crosshairs for spying on Congress, ex-prosecutor Jack Smith and his team monitored the activities of President Donald Trump’s legal defense team, journalists, and campaign advisers using a pen register device that tracked the calls coming to and from his chief of staff Susie Wiles’ phone, according to newly declassified memos that reveal some of the FBI’s invasive tactics used to target Trump," the White House announced in a statement upon the documents' drop on Monday, October 5.

The latest memos, released by the White House Government Transparency Task Force, claim FBI agents assigned to Smith’s investigation cast a sweeping surveillance net during the 2024 election, combing through phone records, social media activity, political endorsements, and other constitutionally protected conduct as investigators probed whether Trump broke the law by taking classified documents to Mar-a-Lago after leaving office in 2021.Trump Probe 'Approved At The Highest Levels of the Biden Justice Department'The White House noted that the three-year probe "was approved at the highest levels of the Biden Justice Department, including by Attorney General Merrick Garland, Deputy Attorney General Lisa Monaco and FBI Director Christopher Wray, the memos show."

It noted that the operation "put Joe Biden’s administration in charge of the legal fate of his GOP rival in the 2024 election," referring to what ultimately became Vice President Kamala Harris's unsuccessful run against The Don after Biden was forced to drop out over questions about his mental acuity.Melania and Barron Trump's Movements Were Surveilled by Biden's FBIA newly surfaced May 2022 email exchange between redacted FBI agents reveals investigators were meticulously mapping out the Trump family’s movements as they prepared to escalate the Mar-a-Lago documents probe.

The agents' checklist included putting the finishing touches on a search warrant, coordinating with federal prosecutors in Florida, and determining exactly how Donald, Melania, and Barron were traveling, down to the type of aircraft and specific timeline. The final marching orders were to “swear out the warrant” and lock down coordination between the FBI, Justice Department, and Secret Service in West Palm Beach.

Another document read, “Any search warrants would be served after the former President departs Mar-a-Lago,” making sure the home was clear of the Trumps before it was executed.Then-Trump Campaign Manager Susie Wiles Had Her Phone Data TappedBut a month before agents descended on Mar-a-Lago, an unnamed FBI special agent reportedly pumped the brakes, questioning whether the bureau even had the legal authority to search the former president’s private office and bedroom and urging further talks with Trump’s attorneys before taking the extraordinary step.

When agents carried out the raid, both Donald and Melania's bedrooms were tossed looking for evidence, along with the 45th president's office. 

The FBI’s alleged surveillance sweep went all the way to Donald himself, with agents painstakingly logging his calls with then-campaign manager Wiles, even flagging the former president’s mysterious "vanity number," a customized phone number that spells out a memorable word.

While the records keep Trump’s personalized digits under wraps, they tracked his calls down to the second. One May 19, 2023, entry coldly clocked: "2:05 pm The FPOTUS Vanity Number called WILES for 16 minutes and 11 seconds."

"Jack Smith’s surveillance operation was a disgraceful abuse of government power," White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement about the newly released documents.

She added, "Spying on political opponents is weaponization of law enforcement, plain and simple. Those responsible must be held accountable."

news.title: Trump’s approval hits new low among Hispanic voters ahead of midterms  - St. Vincent Tribune – Daily St
news.text:
A new poll from the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos has found that United States President Donald Trump’s approval rating remains at a record low as the midterm elections approach in November.

The six-day survey, completed on Monday, found that just 32 percent of US voters approve of the job Trump is doing as president.

While that low rate has held steady since September, the latest Reuters-Ipsos poll suggests his support among Latino voters is continuing to slide.

Trump’s approval rating shrunk this month to 24 percent among Hispanic voters, its lowest point in either of his two terms in office.

The Republican leader had previously made substantial inroads with that constituency.

The Pew Research Center estimated that Trump and his Democratic rival, Kamala Harris, were within three percentage points of each other in the 2024 presidential race, earning 48 percent and 51 percent of the Hispanic vote, respectively.

That rate marked a significant jump for Trump over the 2020 election, when he only earned 36 percent of the Hispanic vote.

Experts have credited the boost in Hispanic support with helping Trump win the 2024 race. His 2020 bid, by contrast, ended in defeat to Democrat Joe Biden.

The Monday poll found that Trump’s gains among Hispanics have largely evaporated.

About 52 percent plan to vote for the Democrats in the November midterms, compared to 26 percent for Republicans.

The upcoming midterm is largely viewed as a referendum on Trump’s second term and will decide whether the Republicans maintain their majorities in the US House of Representatives and the Senate.

Democrats have seized on Trump’s low approval ratings, hoping to translate frustration with the president into voter momentum for their party.

A Democratic majority in one or both houses of Congress would place substantial constraints on Trump’s agenda for the remainder of his time in office.

But Trump has also faced rumblings from within his Republican Party as the November 3 midterms approach.

One Republican incumbent, Representative Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida, released a campaign advertisement last month that addressed Trump directly, saying, “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”

She cited Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown as a source of tension. “Some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” she said, pointing to the detention and deportation of immigrants with no criminal record.

Experts have also warned that the president’s shrinking popularity, driven in part by concerns about the cost of living and his decision to launch a war on Iran, could weigh down Republican candidates in key races across the country.

Still, Trump has continued to express confidence about the prospects of his Republican Party in the upcoming midterms.

He has also defended his decision to place himself at the centre of the Republican election campaign strategy. Trump recently launched a 32-day blitz of cross-country rallies ahead of the November 3 midterms.

“Just so you understand, they all want me to go,” Trump said, denying that some Republicans would prefer he keep his distance. “They all want me to go campaign.”
